nodes.label: DMV official info site www.dmv.ca.gov - not the friendliest site but has official info and appointment system
Link: How to Register Vehicles Purchased in Private Sales - California DMV
DMV appointment: you don't need to bring the seller along
Caveat: you can go to DMV without an appointment, but be prepared to wait
Transfer and registration fee depends on several factors, usually ~10% of the value of the sale
DMV registration fee calculator: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/dmv/detail/portal/feecalculatorweb
You must pay on your appointment day and be prepared to present paperwork to transfer title and update the name on registration
California certificate of title (Pink Slip)
Caveat: if the Pink Slip does not have form fields for ownership transfer and odometer reading, you need form REG 262 from the DMV
Bill of sale form link: http://dmv.ca.gov/forms/reg/reg135.htm

Statement of facts (REG 256) - completed by buyer when vehicle is a gift, sale from family member, smog check exemption, or other differentiating factors; link https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/dmv/?1dmy&urile=wcm:path:/dmv_content_en/dmv/forms/reg/reg256
Proof of insurance required as part of registration paperwork
Liability (3rd party) insurance: covers damage you cause in an accident to other cars and people
Car insurance: covers the damage to your own car if you caused the accident
Caveat: California's law-mandated insurance minimums are very low and will hardly cover you if you get into an accident - make sure you fully understand your coverage
Insurance provider: www.geico.com
Insurance provider: www.aaa.com
Insurance provider: getjerry.com
Insurance broker option: AIS
Geico has recently provided competitive rates, particularly for international students without a driving history in the US
Caveat: in the past Geico has accepted foreign driver's licenses as proof of driving experience under the expectation that you get a California driver's license 'soon'
Tip: if you have records of old foreign driver's licenses showing how long you've been driving, Geico may accept it as proof of experience to lower your premium - scan old licenses before you come
Stanford has EV charging stations on campus, but availability can be limited, especially at the mid-rises and EVGR
Tip: check the specific charging infrastructure at your housing location before committing to an EV
For weekend trips to Tahoe, Yosemite, or Big Sur, range and charging stop planning become important for EVs
Caveat: most EV owners find it manageable, but it requires more planning than a gas car
Purchase parking permit at Stanford Parking & Transportation Services if you get a car and will park on campus
Parking spaces are almost all marked by zone (e.g. A, C, SO, EA); permit gives access to a specific zone determined by housing/commuter status and willingness to pay
Parking permits cost from $300/year for a residential permit (SO, ES etc.) and C commuter permits, up to $1,000/year for A commuter permits
Daily, monthly, and 10-month permit periods are also available
Visitors can park in hourly metered spaces using the Parkmobile mobile app (US credit/debit card required)
Caveat: you cannot park on campus without the relevant zone permit and can be charged up to several hundred dollars for a violation - get a permit as soon as you move your car onto campus
Example: if you live in Escondido Village you need an ES permit; Munger residents get an SO permit
Tip: check the sign where you plan to park before going to get your permit; also check the necessary permit type on the map link
You're only allowed to keep one motorized vehicle on campus unless you're in couples or family housing
Enforcement: 'A', 'C', and 'shared' resident/commuter lots enforced Monday-Friday, 6 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Implication: much available parking space frees up after hours and on weekends for A/C/shared lots
Resident lots posted as 'EA', 'ES', 'SO', 'WE', 'SJ', and 'SH' are enforced 24/7
Parking meters are enforced 8:00 AM - 4:00 PM, Monday - Friday (excl. holidays)
Useful link: Stanford Parking & Transportation Services Website
Useful link: Parking at Stanford | Transportation - more info on permits and all information on Parking @ Stanford
Career Matters section: international students may have additional questions re: pivoting to the U.S. or job search outside the U.S.
CMC and International Committee designed programs: U.S. style networking workshop, global alumni connect, international student panel, plus broadly applicable newsletter and CMC club programs
Tip: keep a lookout for career events after the Academic Adjustment Period ends
CMC international student advisor: Sherice Torres
CMC international student advisor: Deb Aliprandi
These two advisors focus on U.S. visa and work approval process, job search in the U.S. as an international, and global job search
Caveat: any role/function-focused CMC advisor should be able to give tailored advice if you let them know you are international students
Regional club: Europe club
Regional club: MENA club
Regional club/association: SABSA
Regional club/association: ABSA
Caveat: you will not have access to most career resources before the Academic Adjustment Period ends, but you can still use the time to learn from classmates' career paths and reflect/plan
GSB has a very diverse community and chances are someone has been in the community/role/company/industry you're interested in - never hesitate to reach out
Arrillaga Center for Sports and Recreation is the main gym closest to GSB - has weight rooms, cardio equipment, basketball courts, indoor track, and a pool
AOERC (Arrillaga Outdoor Education and Recreation Center) is another option with fitness equipment
Access gym facilities by swiping your Stanford ID (SUID) - no additional membership needed for basic gym use
Schwab Residential Center has a small gym (enough for 4-5 people at once) with treadmill, cable machine, bench, weights, leg press, etc.

Cardinal Pass program: Stanford Recreation and Wellness group fitness classes (yoga, spinning, HIIT, Pilates, etc.), requires a quarterly fee - check https://rec.stanford.edu/move/fitness for current pricing and schedules
Platinum Pass option includes premium classes and F45 membership
Stanford has intramural leagues for soccer, basketball, volleyball, softball, and more; GSB students form teams every quarter - watch for sign-ups on Slack and Blast
Club sports (rugby, cricket, sailing, climbing, etc.) open to graduate students - see https://stanfordclubsports.com/ for the full list
The Gear Hub rents camping gear, ski equipment, surfboards, paddleboards, and more at very affordable rates - https://rec.stanford.edu/adventure/equipment-rentals
Gear Hub is great for Tahoe trips, Big Sur camping, and Santa Cruz surfing
AOERC also has a fully fledged climbing wall which is quite popular among GSB students
Partners with a Stanford Courtesy ID card can access recreational facilities - check with RecWell for current guest pass policy: https://rec.stanford.edu/visit/membership/guest-passes
Some students use ClassPass to access boutique fitness studios (Barry's, CorePower Yoga, etc.) in Palo Alto and the broader Bay Area
Caveat: ClassPass is a personal expense but can be a nice complement to on-campus facilities
First quarter core courses: Accounting, Finance, Organizational Behavior, and Operations (OSM)
Caveat: placement exams before classes start determine Base/Accelerated/Advanced levels for your SECOND quarter core courses, NOT first
If you have strong prior knowledge in a subject, you may be placed at a higher level
Two windows to request a level change (up or down): one in early August and another on the first day of classes; you will need to justify your request
Tip: it is generally recommended to get into levels which you find comfortable so that you can be stress free
GSB has a device-free classroom policy for most first-year core classes - no laptops or phones during class
Caveat: not all professors allow taking notes on your tablet - recommend going through each class's course policy / checking with the professor
You will generally need to take handwritten notes given the device-free policy
Tip: do not rush to buy textbooks before the first day of class - wait until your professors confirm what is required
Caveat: some courses use digital platforms (e.g. MyLab Finance) that require a paid account
You can find almost all textbooks through the Stanford library's website: Stanford Libraries
Physical textbook option: Stanford Bookstore (may offer used copies)
Physical textbook option: buying from MBA2s on the #all-buy-sell Slack channel or WhatsApp
Physical textbook option: Amazon
In many courses, readings are provided digitally through Canvas

Caveat: AI usage policies vary by professor and are evolving - most professors allow AI for brainstorming and assignments, given that you properly cite AI usage in your work; very few (rare) prohibit it entirely
Tip: pay close attention to each course's honor code and AI policy statement at the beginning of the quarter
First-year core class attendance is mandatory - you are expected to attend every class session
Each course has its own policy on excused absences (typically 1-2 per quarter) for documented reasons like illness, family emergencies, or job interviews
Caveat: missing class for personal travel, weddings, or conferences is generally not excused during the first quarter
Tip: if you have a known conflict (e.g. a family wedding), speak with professors early
Caveat: after the first quarter, attendance policies vary by course

CAPS (Counseling and Psychological Services) immediate mental health support phone: 650-723-3785, available 24/7 - a clinician will assess your situation and offer support and/or follow-up recommendations
Embedded CAPS psychologist dedicated to GSB students: Dr. Tom Ellis, email tsellis@stanford.edu
Embedded CAPS psychologist dedicated to GSB students: Dr. Liz Chaney, email lchaney@stanford.edu
Schedule appointments with Dr. Ellis or Dr. Chaney by calling Vaden or emailing them directly for a consultation
TimelyCare Therapy: CAPS offers students up to 12 free virtual therapy sessions with a therapist, paid for by CAPS - accessed through the TimelyCare App
Peer Mentor: you will be assigned a Peer Mentor (an MBA2) during Week Zero, there specifically to help you navigate the first-year experience
Caveat: the GSB culture is supportive, but the pace can be relentless - build habits early (exercise, sleep, stay connected with friends and family back home)
Tip: it is okay to say no to events - you do not need to attend everything

Stanford Courtesy (Affiliate) ID card for partners grants access to campus facilities including libraries, gyms, and dining halls; info shared during Arrival Week; SO website (accessible with Stanford login) has detailed instructions

SO Career Resources: GSB and Stanford broader community offer some career resources for partners, typically shared during Arrival Week - ask the Student Support team for the latest (search myGSB for their latest contact details)
SO Community: there is usually a WhatsApp group for SOs and partners - ask during Arrival Week or on Slack to get added; partners often form strong communities of their own
Housing: if living with a partner, you will likely be in EV (mid-rises or low-rises), EVGR, or off-campus housing
Caveat: GSB Residences (Schwab) has limited couples housing - indicate your housing preference early during the lottery

Gym/Rec Access for Partners: Partners with a Courtesy ID can access Stanford recreational facilities - check RecWell's guest pass policy for current details: https://rec.stanford.edu/visit/membership/guest-passes
Form 8843 is Required for ALL F-1 and J-1 students, even with zero US income
Form 8843 is a simple informational form that tells the IRS you were present in the US as an exempt individual (student); it is not a tax return, it is a statement of your presence
You must file Form 8843 every year you are in the US on an F-1 or J-1 visa, regardless of whether you earned any income
Form 8843 is straightforward and takes about 15 minutes to fill out
Download Form 8843 from IRS website: https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8843

Sprintax needed if you earned any US income (from an internship, CPT employment, scholarships/fellowships treated as taxable income, etc.) - you will likely need to file a federal (and possibly state) tax return
Caveat: as a non-resident alien, you cannot use standard tax software like TurboTax
Sprintax is designed specifically for non-resident tax filing

Stanford provides a Sprintax access code that significantly reduces the cost; Bechtel International Center publishes instructions each tax season: https://bechtel.stanford.edu/navigate-international-life/taxes/sprintax-software
Tax filing season runs from January through April 15
You will typically receive your W-2 form (from any US employer) by late January, and then file your return
Tip: there are usually envelopes and stamps available at the Schwab Residences front desk if you need to mail any tax documents
Caveat: apart from Sprintax, there are other tax software options with some free features, however Sprintax is the most reliable for non-resident filings
Tip: if your tax situation is complex (e.g. investment income, income from multiple countries, or tax treaty benefits to claim), consider consulting a tax professional
Stanford's VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) program sometimes offers free tax help
Caveat: verify that VITA volunteers are experienced with non-resident filings
Tip: keep records of any income, tax documents (W-2, 1042-S, 1099), and your entry/exit dates for the US throughout the year - you will need these when filing
International students on F-1 visas are not allowed to work in any form during the first three quarters of the MBA program (Autumn, Winter, Spring)
No-work rule includes full-time work, part-time work, freelancing, consulting, paid referrals, or ANY activity that generates income
The earliest date you can start working is after the official end date of Spring Quarter (refer to the Stanford academic calendar for this date)
Caveat: violating the no-work rule jeopardizes your visa status
CPT (Curricular Practical Training) is the authorization that allows F-1 students to work (e.g. summer internships) as part of their academic program
You will need CPT authorization before you can start any internship
GSB official guide on CPT will be updated every year; current guide linked is for 2026, similar guide expected for 2027 via MyGSB
Document: '2025-2026 CPT Step-by-Step Guide for MBA1s on F1 (MyGSB)'
Tip: when enrolling in the GSBGEN 299 course on Axess-Navigate Enrollment, your default quarter might not be Summer 202X - remember to change the term on the right top corner of Navigate
Screenshot: Navigate 'Select term' dialog showing options Spring 2026 and Summer 2026
Tip: start the CPT application process as soon as you have a confirmed internship offer, since the process takes time
Sequence: you need the CPT-endorsed I-20 before you can apply for an SSN, and you need the SSN before your employer can process your payroll
SSN Eligibility: you can only apply for an SSN within one month of your employment start date
Example: if your internship starts on June 15, the earliest you should schedule an SSN appointment is around May 15
Apply for SSN online at https://secure.ssa.gov/ossnap/public/landingOSsnap or visit a Social Security Administration (SSA) office in person
Caveat: the SSN application website often runs into glitches and may enter a loop of verification or not proceeding to booking appointments
Note: the SSN website glitch sometimes self-resolves and you can proceed normally; people have reported it working better on mobile phones vs desktop/laptops
Tip: if the glitch persists, suggest not to wait and instead visit an SSA office in person as soon as possible
SSN document needed: passport
SSN document needed: I-94, printed from https://i94.cbp.dhs.gov/
SSN document needed: CPT-endorsed I-20
SSN document needed: SSN application form
Caveat: there are often discretionary decisions made by SSA officers too - e.g. you may be asked to present a birth certificate; most of the time, your passport should be fine
Complication example: doing 2 internships in one summer OR changing position or location from the original contract
Tip: for complications, suggest printing out all the related email correspondence as proof
Tip: recommended scheduling an advising appointment with Bechtel in case of any doubts since this is a sensitive topic and every case is unique
Tip: if you cannot find available appointment slots at the SSA office near you, try changing the zip code and checking multiple locations
SSA office with sometimes better availability than Palo Alto-area offices: Redwood City
SSA office with sometimes better availability than Palo Alto-area offices: San Jose
SSA office with sometimes better availability than Palo Alto-area offices: Mountain View
People have also traveled to San Francisco, San Mateo, or Richmond SSA offices depending on which office gives the best timing
Caveat: if the online system does not work, you can try walking into an SSA office in person - this may or may not work depending on the office, but is worth trying if running out of time
Bechtel's full guide on SSN eligibility and application: https://bechtel.stanford.edu/navigate-international-life/social-security-number-ssn
Thanksgiving Break (late November): classes pause for about a week; you can stay in your campus housing; many students travel during this time

Winter Break (mid-December to early January): about 3 weeks; you can stay in campus housing; some students go home, others travel or go on Winter GSTs or stay on campus; campus is quiet and dining options are limited
Spring Break (March): about 10-12 days; this is when the Spring GST typically takes place; you can stay in housing

Summer: housing contracts for the GSB Residences (Schwab and JMac) typically end in June; if you need summer housing (e.g. for an internship in the Bay Area) you will need to arrange a sublease or apply for summer housing separately
You do not need to vacate campus housing during Thanksgiving, winter, or spring breaks
Other help resource: MyGSB website
Admit Support contact: mba_admits@gsb.stanford.edu or +1-650-725-7963 (email preferred)
Bechtel International Center's web page or advising hours: https://bechtel.stanford.edu/

MBA Student Support team helps students sort out any sort of 'life' issues (family, academic, health, etc.) - located on the second floor of the McClelland Building (above the 'M' classrooms in the GSB)

MBA Student Support team knows the University well and will orient you toward relevant resources or may advocate on your behalf; in the first quarter your Academic Advisor will also be a frequent point of contact
MBA Student Support website: https://mygsb.stanford.edu/mba/student-life-home
Emergency support resources list: https://mygsb.stanford.edu/mba/student-life/emergency_support
For MBA students: your Peer Mentor (met during Week Zero) and their 'Ask an MBA2' Slack channel
Your friendly SA International Committee (refer to Part I for names and email addresses)
The international students WhatsApp group (see Part I) - feel free to drop a message whenever in doubt
There is a ~99% chance someone might have the same question as you
General guidance: if you ask any question or support from any MBA2s or staff members, they should at least direct you to the persons who can help if they cannot help you themselves
GSB has a very supportive and tight-knit culture, so never hesitate to ask for help

Many GSB staff members chose their jobs because they like to interact with and support students, and all MBA2s were incoming students themselves too with anxieties and questions addressed by the previous generation - they would love to pay it forward
Closing statement: 'Finally, good luck with the move and we look forward to seeing you on campus!'
GSB centennial marked October 10, 2025 — reunions and panels held in Town Square

nodes.label: Yacht Week logistics lesson: get air conditioning and a host on your boat — without a host you will eat terribly all week

nodes.label: Yacht Week logistics lesson: push for all-GSB boats — people who sailed GSB-only boats stayed friends with boatmates, while mixed boats meant half the crew vanished to HBS afterward
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Yacht Week is where many people find their starting GSB friend group, and it pays off all fall quarter
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: For Colombia, price the operator's add-ons against booking them yourself on Airbnb Experiences or TripAdvisor — the operator's real value is transport and keeping everyone physically together
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Personal opinion: pre-MBA Tahoe is the most skippable of the big three, not because it's bad — Tahoe is a few hours away and you will go all year (Chapter 25), while Yacht Week and Colombia happen exactly once
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Caveat/counterpoint: Tahoe's scale — some classes turn it into a three-hundred-person weekend, its own kind of special
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: If you go to Tahoe, do the three-to-four-day version rather than the two-day one — it's three hours each way on a good day and five in traffic, and two days isn't worth the windshield time
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: A small thing you'll be glad you did: bring a Stanford flag, ideally more than one — every group photo from Yacht Week and Colombia ends up wanting one
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: The Colombia trip runs through an outside operator (VAOVA, in recent years)
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Honest class consensus on Colombia: you're paying a premium, and it's still worth going — what you're buying is transport, the big parties, and several hundred classmates moving as one group; price everything else yourself
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Book the parties; skip the packaged dinners — dinners can be booked yourself at the same restaurants for roughly half the price, in classmates' experience; post the restaurant in the class chat and people will show up
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Worth the upgrade in Colombia: your own bedroom — the 4 a.m. crowd and the 8 a.m.-excursion crowd do not mix well in one room, and a single room costs surprisingly little extra; personal take: skip the premium-hotel upgrade in Cartagena and spend the same money on having your own bedroom instead
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Most day activities are cheaper booked yourself on Airbnb Experiences or TripAdvisor; the catch is rallying people, which is a hassle
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Caveat: be honest about the 8 a.m. options too — plenty of people end up selling their morning slots
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Book the Avianca legs the minute they're released — they can disappear within about fifteen minutes
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Affiliate your United status for better boarding and points on the intermediate legs
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Checking in early for a premium seat runs about $18; first class on the short connecting flights is often only $10–15 more, which is worth it
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: The airport buses leave three to three-and-a-half hours before flights, out of an abundance of caution
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Caveat: plenty of people take a cheap Uber an hour later and sleep in instead — but carry that risk knowingly: if you miss the flight, the operator is not going to rebook you
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Drink bottled water everywhere, and in Cartagena use it to brush your teeth as well — walk to the nearest grocery or convenience store on arrival in each city, buy two big jugs for your room, and grab some fruit; your body will thank you by day four
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Bogotá, Medellín, and Cartagena are three different climates, so packing cubes earn their keep; bring a fan (Cartagena is hot and humid, and the airport has been known to have no air conditioning), shorts for the white party, a flower lei for the flower party, and cough drops
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Sleeper tip: conserve your voice — don't spend every night shouting over the music, talk to the people next to you instead; if you aren't conscious about it, your voice will be gone by the second or third city and you'll croak through the rest of the trip
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Tejo in Medellín — Colombia's national game, gunpowder targets and all, which a local guide will set up and teach; bring cash, around 50,000 COP
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: The Comuna 13 walking tour is worth doing, and worth doing with a good guide
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Some classes have run an unofficial 'shadow trek': booking the same flights, hotels, and cities themselves and traveling alongside the group — cheaper, but the trade-off is real, since you can't sign up for the optional activities or the operator's big parties, so you're on your own to find people for those
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: On the last day, tip the staff and hand over your leftover pesos before you head to the airport, and thank the local guides and drivers — they work hard on that trip
nodes.source_file: assets/Stanford GSB Survival Guide - Completed Version.pdf

nodes.label: Tejo operator (2025 trip): instagram.com/tejo_in_medellin runs a casual teaching session — ask for Chris 'El Gringo,' an expat who plays competitive Tejo; bring 50,000 COP in cash and get to the courts in El Poblado

nodes.label: Housing (Part II, Section 3)
Most common on-campus housing options: Schwab, Jack McDonald Hall, Escondido Village (incl. EVGR), Munger, Oak Creek
Official university housing move-in information is on the Admit Tab of MyGSB
Student Housing website and front desk contacts: https://rde.stanford.edu/studenthousing/
Don't worry if not placed in GSB Residences (Schwab/JMac) - still have access to all social activities and can use their study rooms/amenities

Reasons students prefer not to live in GSB Residences: wanting fresh air outside GSB life, living with significant other (limited couple housing available), having kids, wanting larger space, or saving money for a longer walk/bike ride (10-15 min)
Students in Munger, EV, EVGR or Rains are assigned a Community Associate (CA) - a returning Stanford student who helps build community and assists with transition; info provided at key pickup

nodes.label: Vaccinations (Part II, Section 4.1)
Get required vaccinations and an English translation of immunization record at a hospital in home country before coming to GSB
Stanford requires 2 MMR vaccinations given after first birthday and at least 28 days apart
If record shows need for tuberculosis testing, can be taken at home country or Vaden Health Center (appointment required)
MMR vaccine proof and TB test are both required to enroll at the University
Vaden Health Center address: 866 Campus Drive, Stanford, CA 94305
Vaden Health Center appointment phone: (650) 498-2336
Health Insurance (Part II, Section 4.2)
All students (international and domestic) are automatically enrolled in Cardinal Care health insurance plan
Cardinal Care annual premium for 2026-2027 is $8,808 ($734/month), running September 1 through August 31
Cardinal Care is classified as a 'Platinum' plan under the ACA: very high coverage, low out-of-pocket costs (e.g., $50-$100 ER copays, $0 copays for diagnostic labs and X-rays)

To waive Cardinal Care, must do so by early-September (check exact deadline in GSB Digest/MyGSB); Health office makes no exceptions; requires proof of alternative insurance meeting Stanford's minimum standards
More info on Cardinal Care: Vaden website Student Health Matters section, https://vaden.stanford.edu/
Alternative insurance providers used by international students: ISO, Wellaway, PSI, costing $1-3K per annum vs ~$9k for Cardinal Care
Caveat: many alternative insurance plans explicitly exclude skiing as a covered activity - check fine print if planning to ski in Tahoe; people get injured skiing every year
Requirement: alternative insurance plan must include emergency medical evacuation and repatriation coverage for Stanford's waiver standards
Tip: upload insurance brochures to an AI assistant to understand fine print and terms (copay, deductibles, co-insurance, OOP max)
If Cardinal Care is waived, Vaden Health Center basic services are still accessible but billing/coverage works differently

Dependents can sign up for the Stanford Student Dependent Health Insurance Plan (costs/benefits differ from student plan); can only be opted into at first matriculation unless a qualifying life event occurs
Pre-Orientation Trips (Part II, Section 5)
Tahoe Trip: weekend trip to Lake Tahoe organized by MBA2s, usually held the weekend before move-in (early September); most popular pre-orientation event
Colombia Trip: multi-day trip to Colombia organized by students, usually in late August; very popular
Yacht Week: optional trip (typically Croatia or Greece) over the summer with HBS folks; a week of partying on a yacht + beaches; more expensive but memorable
Summer GSTs (Global Study Trips): some GSTs take place over the summer before school starts; academic trips with company visits and cultural experiences

Caveat for international students: F-1 visa holders traveling outside the US between these trips and start of school need a valid travel signature on I-20 and a multi-entry visa; coordinate with Bechtel if unsure
No obligation to attend any/all trips; many international students attend just Tahoe, the most affordable and accessible option

nodes.label: Useful Apps (Part III, Section 6.4)
Uber and Lyft: used constantly for rides
Venmo: essential for student-to-student payments (splitting dinner, event tickets, group trips)

Caveat: Venmo requires a US phone number; $300 weekly spending limit initially, lifted by adding a US bank account and completing identity verification (SSN technically needed to fully verify, but most international students verify without one); transferring funds to bank account takes 2-3 days
Zelle: payment app often built into US banking apps; useful for direct instant bank-to-bank transfers
PayPal: another commonly used payment app
WhatsApp and Slack: group messaging tools used by the GSB class; WhatsApp is the primary tool for student communication
Yelp!: restaurant and services recommendations (hairdresser, dry cleaner, etc.)
Google Maps: navigation, public transit directions, discovering restaurants/stores nearby
Clipper: Bay Area public transit card app (add to Apple/Google Wallet)
DoorDash, Uber Eats: food delivery apps
Instacart: grocery delivery app
Stanford Mobile: contains virtual ID card, events information, etc.
Furniture & Housewares (Part III, Section 7.1)
IKEA (1700 East Bayshore Rd, East Palo Alto)
Caveat: at the start of the academic year, IKEA delivery times can be much longer than usual and popular student-dorm items sell out; go multiple times or order early
Walmart (600 Showers Dr, Mountain View)
Target (555 Showers Dr, Mountain View)
Note: can use delivery service instead of visiting the store in-person
Note: GSB Residences and many other graduate housing options come semi-furnished; check RD&E website (https://rde.stanford.edu) for details

Stanford's Loan Closet lends household items (kitchenware, small appliances, organizers) to students for free on a temporary basis (1-2 years); one-time registration fee of ~$20; check GSB Residences front desk or R&DE for availability

At the start of each academic year, returning students/recent graduates donate kitchenware, furniture, and household items; a sale or giveaway event in the first week offers pots, pans, utensils cheaply; watch GSB Digest/Slack/WhatsApp
Electronics stores (Part III, Section 7.2)
Best Buy (2460 E Charleston Rd, Mountain View)
Apple Store (340 University Ave, Palo Alto, and 379 Stanford Shopping Center)
Stanford Bookstore: usually has promotional offers on certain Apple products at start of academic year, plus discounts on Apple retail prices
Online Shopping (Part III, Section 7.3)
Amazon (www.amazon.com): using .edu address, students get free Amazon Prime for six months, giving free two-day shipping plus streaming (TV shows/movies)
SU Post (http://supost.com): site for Stanford community to buy/sell used goods (cars, furniture, bikes, TVs)
Receiving Packages (Part III, Section 7.4)
If living at GSB Residences, front desk collects packages for you during the year; returns can also be processed there

If living in other university housing, packages can be sent directly to your address; caveat: private delivery services (UPS/FedEx) sometimes lack building access or you may not want packages in hallways

Optional service: Graduate Housing Package Center - request a Unit address, register to have packages automatically forwarded to your housing front desk (https://rde.stanford.edu/studenthousing/mail-deliveries)

Amazon Returns: convenient options near campus are Whole Foods on Emerson Street, Palo Alto (QR code, no box needed) and the nearest UPS Store; also Amazon Hub Lockers at various campus locations; GSB Residences mail room can process some returns
Requesting Repairs (Part III, Section 7.5)
Submit a ServiceNow ticket via the Services Portal for defects/malfunctions in university housing
A technician comes to fix the issue within a few days, depending on urgency
Example repair issues: loose/creaky doors, clogged drains, faulty kitchens, broken windows, missing door stops, electrical issues
Repair service is included in housing bill at no additional cost
If living at GSB Residences, contact Schwab reception front desk directly for priority attention to your repair request
TV (Part III, Section 7.6)
GSB Residences come with a TV in each suite, equipped with cable service
Live TV streaming services use the Stanford WiFi network, requiring the TV to be registered on the network; consult housing staff for setup support
Groceries (Part III, Section 8.1)

On campus supermarkets are limited, small and expensive: Market at Munger (near Munger residences) and EVGR Marketplace (at EVGR); most self-cooking students opt for off-campus supermarkets or delivery
Trader Joe's (855 El Camino Real, Palo Alto): small supermarket close to campus, favorite for many GSBers

Costco Wholesale (1000 N Rengstorff Ave, Mountain View): generally cheapest option but requires buying in bulk; requires membership fee for a Costco card; many international students shop with American students who hold membership; has home delivery option
Walmart (600 Showers Dr, Mountain View): has a groceries section, cheap food in smaller quantities, possibly not best for perishables
Target (555 Showers Dr, Mountain View): another US classic with a groceries section
Safeway (325 Sharon Park Dr, Menlo Park or 525 El Camino Real, Menlo Park): more complete offering of quality products
Whole Foods (774 Emerson St, Palo Alto or 4800 El Camino Real, Los Altos): upscale, high quality, wide variety, higher prices
CVS Pharmacy (855 El Camino Real, Palo Alto): close to campus for prescription/OTC drugs and general merchandise
Real Produce Market (501 Oxford Ave, Palo Alto): close to campus, focus on fresh produce and Middle Eastern/European/Indian products
Apni Mandi (1111 W El Camino Real, Sunnyvale): Indian food supermarket chain with free chai and a cafe inside
99 Ranch Market (1350 Grant Road, Mountain View): Asian food supermarket chain, focus on Chinese foods, some East/South-East Asian ingredients
Instacart: popular option to order groceries
Amazon Fresh: Amazon's grocery delivery option, includes delivery from Whole Foods
Weee!: Online Asian supermarket
Arrillaga Family Dining Commons: popular with GSBers, a block from GSB, halfway between GSB Residences and Munger
Wilbur Dining and Stern Dining: slightly further away than Arrillaga, also popular with GSBers
Meal Plan: best value way to pay for dining halls; prepay a block of meals deducted per use; usable at any dining hall; unused amount may be eligible for refund at end of academic year
Coupa Café: decent coffee, good salads/paninis/arepas; open late and weekends during term; three campus locations incl. Knight Management Center; pre-order online for pickup
Caveat: recommended to get a Coupa Café account for seasonal promotions, e.g. a $5 coupon for every $50 spent
Arbuckle Dining Pavilion: heart of Knight Management Center; wide international buffet; salad bar known for low cost/nutrition ratio; open only breakfast and lunch
Jimmy V's Sports Cafe: quick buffet lunches/snacks; in Arrillaga Family Sports Center, across Campus Drive from GSB behind Bass Library; alternative to Arbuckle
Axe & Palm: good burgers and milkshakes, open very late, popular; located in Old Union building near Stanford bookstore and Tresidder Memorial Union on White Plaza
CoHo: good food, very popular, long hours; located in Tresidder Memorial Union with live music in the evenings
Ray's Grill: graduate student pub open long hours and weekends; between Escondido Village and EV South; Mexican and Asian food; good for viewing sports
Union Square: food court in Tresidder Memorial Union with Subway, Panda Express, and Starbucks
DoorDash: popular platform for food delivery
Grubhub: another popular food delivery platform
Ekatree: newer delivery option; reduced fees but fixed delivery times, specific delivery locations across campus, limited restaurant options
Restaurants (sit-down, table service): tip 18-20% of pre-tax bill, not optional
Caveat: when dining in a group, check whether gratuity has already been added (common for groups of 6+)
Coffee shops/fast-casual counters: optional tip, $1-2 or 10-15% appreciated; fine to select "No tip" when just picking up a drink
Uber/Lyft: 10-15% tip typical, tip through the app after the ride
Food delivery (DoorDash, Uber Eats): $3-5 minimum tip, or 15-20% for larger orders
Hair salons/barbers: tip 15-20% of the service cost
Hotels: $2-5/night for housekeeping (left on nightstand), $1-2/bag for bellhops
Movers/furniture delivery: $10-20 per person for large jobs
Taxis: tip 15-20%
Default rule: when in doubt, 15-20% is the safe tip for any service involving a human; tipping done after service rendered, on top of listed price
Purpose of a bank account: wire money from abroad, receive loan funds and Venmo payments, ATM cash access, pay debit where foreign cards not accepted, other transactions
Stanford Federal Credit Union: Tresidder Memorial Union 2nd floor, or 694 Pampus Lane near Escondido Village
SFCU gives Debit card right away and a guaranteed credit card even without credit history/income

SFCU process: open checking account virtually, mail financial aid award letter if received, then in person present fellowship as proof of income, bring passport, RD&E proof of address letter from Axess, and ideally student ID
SFCU 'refer a friend, both get $50' program
Wells Fargo Bank: Tresidder Memorial Union second floor

Citibank: 250 University Ave, Palo Alto or 2401 El Camino Real, Palo Alto; has provided credit cards to students without credit history; convenient for transferring funds if already a client back home
Chase: 855 El Camino Real, Bldg 2, Palo Alto
Bank of America: 3000 El Camino Real, Palo Alto (near California Ave); has an ATM on campus at Tresidder Union
Documents likely needed to open a bank account: passport, I-20 or DS-2019, Stanford ID, proof of address (mail/bill, housing front desk letter, or RD&E letter from Axess)
Banks vary: some on/near campus with handy ATMs, others nationally widespread with more ATMs; debit card fees and credit card willingness without credit history vary and change over time

Many students set up a US bank account in their home country before arriving via banks with operations in both countries (e.g. HSBC, Citibank); fees vary by country, ask current/graduating students from your country
Caveat: difficult for International Students to obtain a credit card in the US unless you have credit history or open a US account with your existing bank
However, debit cards obtainable at the listed banks work fine at most stores and online shopping sites that accept credit cards
A good credit score is critical after graduation (e.g. landlords may check credit before signing a lease); takes years to build
You need a Social Security Number (obtained when you start working in the US) before you can generally open a credit card in the US
Entry-level credit card option: apply with Stanford Federal Credit Union (recommended)
Entry-level credit card option: open a credit card with your US bank after opening a checking account there, since they hold your savings

Entry-level credit card option: use statements from a recent corporate credit card in your home country (e.g. American Express) in your name as proof of credit history for a nicer card (no guarantee of success)
Venmo and Zelle are extremely used for student-to-student payments; direct deposits are uncommon in the US
A checkbook might be useful for large payments (e.g. rent if living off-campus, or dealing with non-Stanford agencies)
Credit and debit cards are used very frequently in the US, even for small purchases like coffee; but gas station dispensers and some online stores do not take foreign cards
Traditional bank wire transfers: cost $25-50 per transfer, plus unfavorable exchange rates costing an additional 1-3%

nodes.label: Tip: buy a U-lock - many bike thefts on campus, cable locks aren't safe; lock the frame, not just the tire
Tip: get a helmet - accidents are very common on campus with distracted students riding in many directions
Requirement: must have lights when riding after dark; free lights given when you register your bike
Get your bike registered: it's compulsory and it's your only chance of recovering it if stolen
Caveat: police sometimes stop and fine bikers around the GSB for not stopping at stop signs or not using headlights after dark

E-scooters great for flat campus terrain; consider battery range if riding to hilly destinations (e.g. off-campus)

nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Caveat: cannot get a state-issued ID until you have an active SEVIS record at Bechtel International Center; schedule DMV appointment a few weeks after 'Maintaining Your Legal Status' session at Bechtel
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: DMV first visit documents: unexpired passport, valid US Visa, I-20 or DS-2019, printed I-94, two proof-of-address documents (e.g. bank statements, myHousing portal housing verification letter)
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Caveat: SSN requirement for REAL ID at DMV has been variable/dependent on the DMV officer - some got REAL ID without SSN, others needed SSN for REAL ID but could still get Driving License without REAL ID
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Nonrefundable DMV application fee: approximately $45-50, paid in office (in-person recommended over online due to reported payment technical issues)
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Traffic laws and sign test: computer-based, available in several languages, 36 questions, need at least 30 correct (80%+) to pass, three chances with immediate retake
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Tip: review free California Driver's Handbook (available in other languages at DMV or downloadable); invest 30-60 mins studying; multiple students fail this part each year
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: After passing the written test, you receive a temporary driver's permit allowing you to drive only under supervision of someone with a valid full license; permit number lets you book the behind-the-wheel test
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Behind-the-wheel test: need a car registered in California with registration and insurance card; own car, rental (check policy - Zipcar explicitly disallows use for driving test), or borrowed friend's car
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Requirement: someone with a valid California driver's license must accompany you for the behind-the-wheel test, no exceptions even with a foreign driving license
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Caveat: behind-the-wheel test is not required if you already have a driver's license from another US state
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: After passing the behind-the-wheel test, you get a paper license valid for 90 days while the plastic card is processed
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Foreign applicants' cases go to a back office specialized in immigration matters; most receive cards in 14 days to 1 month; renew paper license at DMV if it takes longer and expiry approaches
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Caveat: if you leave and re-enter the US after the test but before back office review, your submitted I-94 will have expired, which has reportedly stalled applications; not proactively flagged by DMV - visit DMV if in doubt
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: California driver's license valid from day received until academic program end date listed on I-20/DS-2019; renew if you extend your stay
nodes.source_location: 11.2 How to Get a California Driver's License

nodes.label: Tip: wait 10 days after SEVIS record registered/validated by Bechtel before applying for a license; F1 students must attend Maintaining Legal Status session first; records validated by November 1 unless earlier validation requested online via iCenter

Recommendation: apply for a REAL ID instead of just a driver's license - allows domestic flights without a passport; requires same documents plus a second proof of residence (e.g. GSB residences letter, bank statement)
Tip: DMV lines are very long even with an appointment; assume 2-4 hours wait, get there early and bring something to occupy time
Tip: schedule an online DMV appointment early - slots usually available several weeks into the future
Tip: don't schedule/visit the DMV during Week 0 or Week 1; do it during Arrival Week or once class schedule is known; no need to stress if not done early
Many students don't buy a car, especially in first year - campus is walkable/bike-friendly, services nearby, online economy booming
Buy a used car via your own network: recent alums, country/region distribution lists, or Slack
kbb.com: great place to check average market price for used cars
cargurus.com: online used car listing site
cars.com: online used car listing site
sfbay.craigslist.org: lots of variety for used cars, but a wild market
Dealers often offer significant discounts on Labor Day (first Monday in September)
You should take the car to a mechanic for evaluation before buying
Carfax (carfax.com): online registry most reputable mechanic shops report to; checks for accidents, major repairs, completed recalls
Price check: compare prices using kbb.com, cargurus.com, or cars.com to ensure not overpaying
dmv.ca.gov: official California DMV site for car registration information and appointments
Make a DMV appointment to register and title the vehicle in your name; seller does not need to come; walk-in possible but expect a wait
Transfer and registration fees: usually ~10% of the sale value; use DMV's registration fee calculator to estimate
California certificate of title (Pink Slip): if it lacks fields for ownership transfer/odometer reading, need form REG 262 from the DMV
Bill of sale form (REG 135) required for car registration paperwork
Statement of facts form (REG 256): completed by buyer when vehicle is a gift, family sale, smog check exemption, or other differentiating factors
Proof of insurance required to register the car
Liability (3rd party) insurance: covers damage you cause in an accident to other cars and people
Car insurance (collision): covers damage to your own car if you caused the accident
Caveat: law-mandated minimum insurance coverage in California is very low and will hardly cover you in an accident - understand your coverage fully

Geico (geico.com): has recently provided competitive rates for international students without US driving history; has accepted foreign driver's licenses and old license records as proof of driving experience to lower premiums, expecting a CA license 'soon'
Other insurance purchase options: aaa.com, getjerry.com, or through a broker such as AIS
Tip: scan old foreign driver's licenses before coming to the US as proof of driving duration for insurance premium purposes

Electric Vehicles: Stanford has campus charging stations but availability can be limited, especially at mid-rises and EVGR; check charging infrastructure before committing to an EV; range/charging planning important for Tahoe, Yosemite, Big Sur trips
A parking permit is required to park a car on campus, giving access to a specific zone (e.g. A, C, SO, EA)
Parking permits cost from $300 for residential permits (SO, ES, etc.) and C commuter permits, up to $1,000 per year for A commuter permits; daily, monthly, and 10-month options also available
Parkmobile mobile app: visitors can park in hourly metered spaces, US credit/debit card required
Warning: cannot park without the relevant zone permit, can be charged several hundred dollars for a violation
Permit type/price depends on housing location (e.g. Escondido Village needs ES permit, Munger needs SO permit); check the sign where you plan to park
Rule: only one motorized vehicle allowed on campus unless in couples or family housing
'A', 'C', and 'shared' resident/commuter lots enforced Monday-Friday, 6 a.m. to 4 p.m.; much space frees up after hours and on weekends
Resident lots 'EA', 'ES', 'SO', 'WE', 'SJ', 'SH' are enforced 24/7
Parking meters enforced 8:00 AM - 4:00 PM, Monday - Friday, excluding holidays

Career Management Center (CMC) and International Committee designed programs for international students: U.S.-style networking workshop, global alumni connect, international student panel, newsletters, career club programs
CMC has two specific advisors for international students: Sherice Torres and Deb Aliprandi, focused on US visa/work approval process, US job search, and global job search
Regional clubs/associations (e.g. Europe club, MENA club, SABSA, ABSA) are a resource for career interest in a specific region
Caveat: most career resources are inaccessible before the Academic Adjustment Period ends, but you can still learn from classmates' career paths and start planning during this time
Arrillaga Center for Sports and Recreation: main gym closest to GSB; weight rooms, cardio equipment, basketball courts, indoor track, pool; free with SUID
AOERC (Arrillaga Outdoor Education and Recreation Center): another gym option with fitness equipment and a fully fledged climbing wall
Access these gym facilities by swiping your Stanford ID; no additional membership needed for basic gym use
Schwab Residential Center gym: small (enough for 4-5 people at once) with treadmill, cable machine, bench, weights, leg press
Cardinal Pass program: paid group fitness classes (yoga, spinning, HIIT, Pilates) via Stanford Recreation and Wellness; requires quarterly fee, check rec.stanford.edu/move/fitness for pricing
Platinum Pass option: includes premium classes and F45 membership
Stanford intramural leagues: soccer, basketball, volleyball, softball, and more; GSB students form teams every quarter, sign-ups on Slack and Blast
Club sports (rugby, cricket, sailing, climbing, etc.) open to graduate students; see stanfordclubsports.com for full list
The Gear Hub (Stanford's Outdoor Recreation program): rents camping gear, ski equipment, surfboards, paddleboards at affordable rates; good for Tahoe trips, Big Sur camping, Santa Cruz surfing
Partners with a Stanford Courtesy ID card can access recreational facilities; check RecWell's current guest pass policy
ClassPass: used by some students to access boutique fitness studios (Barry's, CorePower Yoga) in Palo Alto and Bay Area; personal expense, complements on-campus facilities

Course Placement: first quarter core courses in Accounting, Finance, Organizational Behavior, Operations (OSM); placement exams before classes determine Base/Accelerated/Advanced levels for second-quarter quantitative courses
Level change requests (up or down) have two windows: early August and the first day of classes; you must justify your request
Device-Free Classroom policy for most first-year core classes: no laptops or phones; not all professors allow tablet notes - check each class's policy; generally need handwritten notes
Textbooks: do not buy before professors confirm requirements; some courses use paid digital platforms (e.g. MyLab Finance); find textbooks via Stanford Libraries website
Physical textbook options: Stanford Bookstore (may offer used copies), MBA2s on #all-buy-sell Slack channel or WhatsApp, Amazon; readings often provided digitally through Canvas

AI in the Classroom: policies vary by professor and are evolving; most allow AI for brainstorming/assignments with proper citation, very few prohibit it entirely; check each course's honor code and AI policy statement
First-year core class attendance is mandatory; each course allows typically 1-2 excused absences per quarter for documented reasons (illness, family emergencies, job interviews)

Caveat: missing class for personal travel, weddings, or conferences is generally not excused during the first quarter; speak with professors early if you have a known conflict; policies vary by course after the first quarter
Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS): available 24/7 at 650-723-3785 for immediate mental health support; clinician assesses situation and offers support/follow-up recommendations
Dr. Tom Ellis and Dr. Liz Chaney are embedded CAPS psychologists dedicated to GSB students; schedule via Vaden or email tsellis@stanford.edu or lchaney@stanford.edu
TimelyCare Therapy: CAPS offers up to 12 free virtual therapy sessions with a therapist, paid for by CAPS, accessed through the TimelyCare App
Peer Mentor (an MBA2) assigned during Week Zero, there to help navigate the first-year experience
Advice: build habits early - exercise, sleep, stay connected with friends/family back home; okay to say no to events, no need to attend everything
Stanford Courtesy (Affiliate) ID card: partner can obtain this, grants access to libraries, gyms, dining halls; instructions shared during Arrival Week via SO website
SO Career Resources: GSB and Stanford community offer some career resources for partners, typically shared during Arrival Week; ask Student Support team for latest via myGSB
SO Community: usually a WhatsApp group for SOs/partners; ask during Arrival Week or on Slack to join; partners often form strong communities
Partner housing: likely EV (mid-rises/low-rises), EVGR, or off-campus; GSB Residences (Schwab) has limited couples housing; indicate housing preference early during the lottery
Partners with Courtesy ID can access Stanford recreational facilities; check RecWell's guest pass policy for current details

Form 8843: required for all F-1 and J-1 students even with zero US income; informational form stating presence as exempt individual; not a tax return; takes about 15 minutes; must file every year on F-1/J-1; download from irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8843
Sprintax: tax filing software for non-resident aliens with US income (from internship, CPT employment, taxable scholarships/fellowships); standard software like TurboTax cannot be used

Stanford provides a Sprintax access code that significantly reduces cost; Bechtel International Center publishes instructions each tax season at bechtel.stanford.edu/navigate-international-life/taxes/sprintax-software
Tax filing season runs January through April 15; W-2 form from any US employer typically received by late January, then file your return
Tip: envelopes and stamps usually available at Schwab Residences front desk for mailing tax documents
Other tax software options with some free features exist apart from Sprintax, but Sprintax is most reliable for non-resident filings

Stanford's VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) program sometimes offers free tax help; verify volunteers are experienced with non-resident filings; consider a tax professional for complex situations (investment income, multiple countries, tax treaty benefits)
Keep records of income, tax documents (W-2, 1042-S, 1099), and US entry/exit dates throughout the year for filing

F-1 students are not allowed to work in any form (full-time, part-time, freelancing, consulting, paid referrals, any income-generating activity) during the first three quarters (Autumn, Winter, Spring); earliest work start is after Spring Quarter's official end date; violating jeopardizes visa status
Curricular Practical Training (CPT): authorization allowing F-1 students to work (e.g. summer internships) as part of academic program; required before starting any internship
GSB official CPT guide updated yearly; 2025-2026 CPT Step-by-Step Guide for MBA1s on F1 available on MyGSB - Career - International Resources
Tip: when enrolling in GSBGEN 299 on Axess-Navigate Enrollment, remember to change the default term (top right corner) to Summer 202X
Start CPT application as soon as you have a confirmed internship offer; process takes time; need CPT-endorsed I-20 before applying for SSN, and SSN before employer can process payroll
SSN eligibility: can only apply within one month of employment start date (e.g. internship starting June 15 -> earliest appointment around May 15)

Apply for SSN online at secure.ssa.gov/ossnap/public/landingOSsnap or visit an SSA office in person; website often has verification loop glitches, sometimes self-resolves, reportedly works better on mobile than desktop
Caveat: if the SSN application website glitch persists, visit an SSA office in person as soon as possible instead of waiting

SSN documents needed: passport, I-94 (printed from i94.cbp.dhs.gov), CPT-endorsed I-20, SSN application form; officers may discretionarily ask for a birth certificate; provide email correspondence as proof for complications like dual internships or changed position/location; recommend an advising appointment with Bechtel for doubts

Tip: if no appointment slots near you, try changing zip code and checking multiple locations; Redwood City, San Jose, Mountain View offices sometimes have better availability than Palo Alto-area; people have traveled to San Francisco, San Mateo, or Richmond
If online SSA system doesn't work, try walking into an office in person; may or may not work depending on office, worth trying if running out of time
Bechtel's full guide on SSN eligibility and application: bechtel.stanford.edu/navigate-international-life/social-security-number-ssn
Thanksgiving Break (late November): classes pause about a week; can stay in campus housing; many students travel

nodes.label: Winter Break (mid-December to early January): about 3 weeks; can stay in campus housing; some go home, others travel or do Winter GSTs or stay on campus; campus quiet, dining limited
nodes.source_location: Part IV.3 Housing During Academic Breaks

nodes.label: Spring Break (March): about 10-12 days; Spring GST typically takes place; can stay in housing
nodes.source_location: Part IV.3 Housing During Academic Breaks

nodes.label: Summer: GSB Residences (Schwab and JMac) housing contracts typically end in June; need to arrange sublease or apply for summer housing separately if needed (e.g. for a Bay Area internship)

nodes.label: You do not need to vacate campus housing during Thanksgiving, winter, or spring breaks

Navigation convention: each chapter banner carries ← (previous chapter), S (back to Contents), and → (next chapter); chapter titles link back to their Contents line; every "Chapter N" mention is a live link; page headers name the current chapter; PDF sidebar carries the full outline

The guide follows the arc of your time at the GSB, organized in three parts
Part I — Before You Arrive: packing, getting here, housing, insurance, money, and phones; read the summer before you land

Part II — Life at the GSB: the big middle covering room, food, tech, communication channels, academics, careers, social life, trips, health, getting around, local services, significant others, international students, and looking after yourself; skim early, come back as chapters become relevant
Part III — Exiting the GSB: the summer between years, second year, and graduation — the things everyone wishes they had known three months earlier

Companion Resources folder holds original attachments (health-insurance comparison spreadsheet, packing list, Blast FAQ, several official PDFs); lives in a public Google Drive folder open to anyone with the link, no Stanford login needed; every reference in the guide links directly to the file; Appendix A lists everything in it
Each Part opens with an Essentials page — the handful of things to read if you read nothing else
Fastest route: feed the guide into an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — the PDF works well) and simply ask it questions; it answers with the guide's specifics and points to the right chapter
Any print shop will spiral-bind the digest-sized PDF for about fifteen dollars; makes a decent gift for an admit

Attribution convention: advice drawn from named, passed-down guides is credited inline; advice from the class's group chats appears uncited by design, with a collective thank-you in the Acknowledgments (apologies to anyone missed)

Prices and dates convention: anything with a dollar sign was true in the 2025–26 academic year (or marked with its own year) and will drift; one-off events and dated deadlines are cut; recurring patterns (e.g. "registration opens in late February") are kept as patterns, not promises

Links convention: hyperlinks preserved throughout including long Amazon product links and passed-down Google Docs, on the theory a working link beats a pretty one; many require a SUNet login; a few will inevitably rot — search MyGSB for the current page when one does

Accuracy note: guide sourced from a great deal of information compiled at a single point in time; verify against the GSB Student Support office, peer mentors, and current MBA2s if anything seems confusing or off; many linked pages get updated (and some don't) — check the date on anything official

Completeness note: tips deliberately compiled to include more ideas rather than fewer, so readers get many students' takes side by side; not every tip has been personally tested by the author, and plenty are individual opinions

Nothing in this guide is official. When this document and a Stanford or GSB office disagree, the office is right. For visas and taxes specifically, only Bechtel International Center and a tax professional count

Guide compiled overwhelmingly from the generosity of classmates — in advice chats, on Blast and Slack, in passed-down documents, and in hallway answers to one more question; a companion document records who contributed what
