nodes.label: Pack what is expensive, hard to replace, or needed the day you arrive — plus personal items (photos, small decorations) that make a dorm room feel like yours; nearly everything else can be bought within a 15-minute drive or delivered in two days
The GSB dress code is very relaxed — t-shirts and athleisure are the norm — but bring formal outfits for interviews and formal GSB events

Unofficial wardrobe calendar: Halloween costumes in fall; something sparkly for Vegas FOAM in winter; formalwear (long gowns, suits) for the Winter Formal in winter and GSB Prom in spring; national dress or costumes for many themed parties in between
Despite the sunny brochures, Palo Alto gets cold from November to February, especially at night — pack sweaters and a real coat
Bring a refill of any prescriptions so there's no pharmacy scramble on arrival, and a paper copy of your eyeglass prescription — eye exams in the US are expensive
Tahoe is three hours away, Santa Cruz has surf, and the redwoods have world-class trails — if you own gear you love, bring it; campus sports infrastructure is extensive
International students: bring at least one US-mains adapter for day one; consider replacing cheap electronics in the US rather than hauling a bag of adapters
Packing advice drawn from the International Student Handbook

GSB Residences rooms come with more than expected: shared kitchens include a two-burner stove, oven, refrigerator/freezer, microwave, garbage disposal, kitchen table and chairs, and a compost bin on request; studios come furnished with the basics
A room-by-room packing list — split into “provided by GSB Residences,” “ship to school,” and “buy at school” — is in the Resources folder as “GSB Residences Packing List.xlsx”

GSB Residences accept packages a few days before move-in (front desks process deliveries year-round once you're in); other residences vary — confirm with your front desk before shipping; official move-in info lives on MyGSB

Linens and towels are not provided for day one; order online for delivery to your dorm or pack one set; many pre-order basics from IKEA, but at term start IKEA delivery slows down and dorm staples sell out — order early

International shipping via UPS/FedEx/DHL is expensive; check your home-country airlines' cargo divisions (e.g. Lufthansa Cargo, Delta Cargo), or ask an MBA2 or California-based classmate to accept boxes
Forgot something? A Stanford email historically gets a free six-month Amazon Prime student trial (terms change — check current); Chapter 9 has the complete move-in shopping map

Shipping a car across the country comes up at both ends of the two years (arrival and the post-graduation scramble east); classmates recommend Montway (praised on price and speed) and McCollister's — get a couple quotes since prices are brokered and swing with the season and route
Most people fly into SFO (closer, more international routes) or SJC (often calmer and closer to the South Bay)

Uber/Lyft — SFO to campus runs roughly $40–$100 depending on surge, about 30 minutes without traffic and up to an hour in rush hour; download both apps before you land, shared-ride tiers save money when offered
Taxi — around $100 plus tip from SFO; rideshare is almost always the better deal

Public transit (cheapest, slowest, rough with a year of luggage — 1 hour+): from SFO take BART to Millbrae then a southbound Caltrain to Palo Alto; from SJC take VTA to Santa Clara station then a northbound Caltrain to Palo Alto; from Palo Alto station, the free Marguerite shuttle, a rideshare, or a ~10-minute cab reaches campus
The Marguerite is Stanford's free public bus — anyone can hop on, no ID needed; connects campus with the Palo Alto Caltrain station and runs several routes used all year (some handy for groceries)
Caltrain itself is free for Stanford students through the Go-Pass — one of the best-kept transit secrets on campus
If you arrive before your housing contract starts, Airbnb and Stanford's visitor-lodging list cover the gap
Driving to SFO instead? Long-term parking sits just past the airport with the AirTrain running from the garage to the terminals; spots can be reserved in advance, though walk-ups usually work

Arrive early if you possibly can — Week Zero is a wall of admin, IT setup, and social events; you do not want to be assembling furniture during it. Aim to have your apartment functional before Welcome Weekend

If you'll have real furniture to assemble or a genuine move, outsource it — a TaskRabbit for assembly or a two-person moving crew for a few hundred dollars is well worth skipping the Week-Zero scramble
The big three pre-MBA trips are Yacht Week, Colombia, and pre-MBA Tahoe; one classmate enjoyed doing all three — it's pretty special to travel with a hundred-plus future classmates

Some Global Study Trips also run as pre-MBA options; good reviews for the opposite reason as the big trips — ~30 people instead of several hundred, a very good size for finding your first friend group

The trips are complements, not substitutes: Yacht Week boats and the Tahoe houses build depth (small, automatic social circles); Colombia is unstructured breadth, meeting people at a rapid rate. One alum's verdict: the yacht-week core group “anchored me on the Colombia trip as I branched out”

Yacht Week logistics: get air conditioning and a host on your boat (without a host you will eat terribly all week); push for all-GSB boats — GSB-only boatmates stayed friends, mixed boats meant half the crew vanished to HBS afterward. Yacht Week is where many find their starting GSB friend group, paying off all fall quarter
For Colombia, price the operator's add-ons against booking them yourself on Airbnb Experiences or TripAdvisor — the operator's real value is transport and keeping everyone physically together

Pre-MBA Tahoe is — in one personal opinion — the most skippable of the three, not because it's bad: Tahoe is a few hours away and you'll go all year (Chapter 25), while Yacht Week and Colombia happen exactly once; the counterpoint is scale — some classes turn it into a three-hundred-person weekend
If you go to pre-MBA Tahoe, do the three-to-four-day version rather than the two-day one — it's three hours each way on a good day and five in traffic, and two days isn't worth the windshield time
Bring a Stanford flag — ideally more than one; every group photo from Yacht Week and Colombia ends up wanting one

The Colombia trip runs through an outside operator (VAOVA, in recent years); class consensus: you're paying a premium, and it's still worth going — you're buying transport, the big parties, and several hundred classmates moving as one group

Book the parties (the reason to pay); skip the packaged dinners — you can book yourself at the same restaurants for roughly half the price, and if you want company, post the restaurant in the class chat

Worth the upgrade: your own bedroom — the 4 a.m. crowd and the 8 a.m.-excursion crowd don't mix well in one room, and a single room costs surprisingly little extra in Colombia; one take: skip the premium-hotel upgrade in Cartagena and spend the money on your own bedroom instead

Most day activities are cheaper booked yourself on Airbnb Experiences or TripAdvisor; the catch is rallying people. Be honest about the 8 a.m. options too — plenty of people end up selling their morning slots

Book the Avianca legs the minute they're released — they can disappear within about fifteen minutes; affiliate your United status for better boarding and points on the intermediate legs. Checking in early for a premium seat runs about $18, and first class on short connecting flights is often only $10–15 more

The airport buses leave three to three-and-a-half hours before flights out of an abundance of caution; plenty of people take a cheap Uber an hour later and sleep in instead — but carry that risk knowingly: if you miss the flight, the operator will not rebook you

Drink bottled water everywhere, and in Cartagena use it to brush your teeth as well; on arriving in each city walk to the nearest grocery/convenience store and buy two big jugs plus some fruit — your body will thank you by day four

Bogotá, Medellín, and Cartagena are three different climates, so packing cubes earn their keep; bring a fan (Cartagena is hot and humid, airport has been known to have no A/C), shorts for the white party, a flower lei for the flower party, and cough drops
Conserve your voice — the sleeper tip. Don't spend every night shouting over the music; talk to the people next to you instead, or your voice is gone by the second or third city
Tejo in Medellín — Colombia's national game, gunpowder targets and all — a local guide will set it up and teach you (bring cash, around 50,000 COP)
The Comuna 13 walking tour is worth doing, and worth doing with a good guide

Some classes have run an unofficial “shadow trek” — booking the same flights, hotels, and cities themselves and traveling alongside the group; cheaper, but the trade-off is real: you can't sign up for the optional activities or the operator's big parties
On the last day, tip the staff and hand over your leftover pesos before you head to the airport, and thank the local guides and drivers — they work hard on that trip

Operator-grade specifics (2025 trip): for Tejo in Medellín, instagram.com/tejo_in_medellin runs a casual teaching session — ask for Chris “El Gringo,” an expat who plays competitive Tejo; bring 50,000 COP cash and get to the courts in El Poblado
In Cartagena, the grocery store beside the Hotel Estelar covers bottled water and every other essential

GSB students live all over: Schwab Residential Center and Jack McDonald Hall (“JMac”) — together “the GSB Residences” — plus Escondido Village Graduate Residences (EVGR) and the mid-rises/low-rises, Munger, Oak Creek and other subsidized off-campus options, and regular Palo Alto apartments

Didn't get the GSB Residences? Genuinely fine — you keep full access to GSB social life and can use the Residences' amenities and study spaces via a quick card-access request; every amenity in JMac or Schwab is available to residents of both

Plenty of students actively prefer EVGR, Munger, or off-campus: more space, fresh air from the GSB bubble, room for a partner or kids (couples housing in the GSB Residences is limited), or lower cost for a slightly longer bike ride; Munger, EV/EVGR, and Rains are all close to the GSB with strong GSB communities
University housing residents get a Community Associate (CA) — a returning Stanford student whose job is to help you settle in and build community; you get their info at key pickup

The GSB Residences (Schwab and JMac): proximity and serendipity — 1 a.m. common-room conversations, every meeting a two-minute walk, peer-mentor culture lives here; rooms include a full XL bed with under-bed storage, desk and office chair, lounge chair with ottoman, TV, space heater; shared kitchens carry a stove, oven, microwave, fridge, table, and stools; honest costs: you can really only work in your room, temperature complaints happen, and the lottery can screw you

Munger trades proximity for livability: a dishwasher, bigger rooms, real hosting space, indoor common rooms, closer to the pool and Tresidder, an MBA2-heavy cross-school community — though you'll commute to spontaneous GSB socializing. Munger and the GSB Residences are the only housing on campus with air conditioning, with the caveat that a Munger quad shares one A/C setting for the whole quad, while GSB Residences rooms control their own

EVGR high-rises — the workhorse choice, especially for second years watching budgets: solid big rooms, the EVGR Pub downstairs, and a relaxed, slightly-outside-the-GSB-gravity feel once you cross the traffic circle — more of the wider grad-student world, a little more sterile
EV mid-rises — the sweet spot for couples without kids: a real step up in space, still close, with a large GSB-couples contingent
Schwab couples housing — unbeatable proximity, but really two Schwab singles joined with one room converted to a living room, at a notably higher price — it is quite expensive

EV low-rises — built for families with kids and incredible bang for the buck: a little farther out, but a no-brainer with a third or fourth family member coming; some couples have gotten lucky and scored a low-rise without a kid
Rains — older and lower-quality, but its low-rise layout breeds real community and hosts a lot of the university's grad-student parties

However the lottery lands, it's fine: non-residents keep full access to GSB social life and can request card access to the Residences; housing for second year is a spring-quarter application (late April/early May) with group mechanics covered in Part III
Stanford student housing is no-pets, full stop — enforcement has teeth: a resident found with an animal is charged $100 per day until it's rehomed
The exceptions are registered service animals and OAE-approved support animals; approval is a real accommodations process, not a formality

If the dog is non-negotiable, R&DE maintains a list of subsidized off-campus apartments that accept pets, and the regular off-campus market is pet-tolerant at a price; decide before you arrive, not after

A note on the numbers: the rent anchors below are 2026 one-bedroom averages from listing-site data (RentCafe, Zumper, Zillow) — sources disagree by hundreds of dollars, so treat them as order-of-magnitude, and treat the vibe summaries as a starting sketch worth checking against a current student's read

Downtown Palo Alto (University Ave): walk-to-everything option, restaurants, bars, class social gravity; priciest per square foot — PA one-bedrooms average roughly $3,100–$4,000 depending on source and block
California Ave / Midtown Palo Alto: quieter, Sunday farmers market, Third Thursdays, fully bikeable to campus; similar prices to downtown with slightly more space
Menlo Park: one-bedrooms around $3,600; the Rosewood/Sand Hill VC corridor on one end, a sleepy downtown on the other; popular with couples and the finance-track crowd

Mountain View: one-bedrooms roughly $3,500–$3,900, but with far more actual apartment stock — newer buildings, amenities, parking; Castro Street is a real downtown and Caltrain makes campus a straight shot
Redwood City: one-bedrooms around $3,400–$3,700 and generally the best value-to-downtown ratio on the list — a revived center, Caltrain stop, 15–20 minutes to campus

East Palo Alto: the lowest rents within biking distance (the IKEA side of the freeway); weigh the specifics of the block — rents, commute, current crime and walkability data — and visit in person before you sign

San Francisco: some MBA2s make the move for spring quarter or the whole second year — the free Caltrain GoPass makes it a ~1-hour door-to-door commute; you trade the serendipity for the city, and do it knowingly, not in your first year
Over all of it: the passdown layer (Chapter 27) — the named houses change the math entirely, because you're not renting an apartment, you're inheriting a social institution

All students are automatically enrolled in Cardinal Care, Stanford's student health plan (administered through Aetna networks) — comprehensive and expensive; enrollment is a full-year commitment through the end of August, with no early-cancellation refunds even if a summer employer covers you
To opt out, you must apply for a waiver by the posted deadline (mid-September for autumn entrants); the health office does not grant exceptions to the deadline. Start at the Vaden insurance overview

One rule that bites people: Cardinal Care (underwritten by Wellfleet) now strictly enforces a referral requirement — as of 2026, nonemergency specialty and off-campus care generally must be referred through Vaden first, or the claim can be denied

A group of students built a side-by-side comparison of Cardinal Care against common alternatives — it lives in the Resources folder as “Health Insurance – Plan Comparison.xlsx”; headline numbers are 2024–25 figures, expect drift, verify current
Cardinal Care: monthly premium ~$635, annual deductible $100, in-network coinsurance 100%, out-of-pocket max $2,000, waiver-eligible: n/a (default)
ISO Care Elite: monthly premium ~$228, annual deductible $40, in-network coinsurance 90%, out-of-pocket max $6,350, waiver-eligible: Yes
ISO Care PSI plans: monthly premium ~$128, annual deductible $500, in-network coinsurance 80%, out-of-pocket max $6,350, waiver-eligible: No
Fourth comparison plan: monthly premium ~$235–$343, annual deductible $250, in-network coinsurance 80%, out-of-pocket max $6,350, waiver-eligible: Was TBC — check

Comparison spreadsheet's conclusion: total “potential” expenses across all plans are broadly similar, but premiums and deductibles vary greatly, so it boils down to risk appetite; when checked, Stanford offered a waiver only for the ISO Elite Care plan, NOT the cheaper Care plan — comparison via Divyansh Agarwal, Soham Saha, and collaborators

International students: waivers additionally require proof of $50,000 medical-evacuation and $25,000 repatriation coverage to home country; J-visa holders need a deductible of $500 or less. Complete the International Student Insurance Coverage Certification Form; decisions come within ~10 business days
Read the exclusions: several cheap plans explicitly exclude skiing injuries. GSB students go to Tahoe constantly and someone gets hurt every year
The Stanford Student Dependent Health Insurance Plan is opt-in and can only be purchased when you first matriculate — your one chance for your entire degree, barring a qualifying life event

European-passport holders: several classmates have waived Cardinal Care in favor of Chapka Student, a French broker (underwritten by AXA) built for students abroad; recent pricing ran roughly €500 a year even over age 30, with no copay, no deductible, and no cap on hospitalization; US network partner UnitedHealthcare, Stanford Health Care in-network; one classmate reported paying nothing on a significant mid-year claim

If you qualify, Chapka can be dramatically cheaper than Cardinal Care — on the order of several thousand dollars a year — while comparably or more comprehensive; but this is one classmate's experience, not a recommendation — confirm the plan clears Stanford's waiver requirements and covers what you'll need (including skiing and treks), because if you waive and a claim is later denied, that risk is entirely yours

Stanford's immunization requirements are broader than the MMR shot most people remember, and missing them triggers a registration hold: two MMR doses (after first birthday, at least 28 days apart), a full Hepatitis B vaccine series plus a positive Hepatitis B surface-antibody titer, and tuberculosis screening; graduate students generally must file any medical or religious exemption by late July
International students: bring an English translation of your immunization record. If TB testing is flagged for you, book it at Vaden Health Center — 866 Campus Drive, appointments at (650) 498-2336
Once here, the Vaden travel clinic can top up any travel vaccines needed for GSTs and treks — cheaper and easier than sorting it abroad
Student refunds (financial aid disbursements, over-payments) are sent to exactly one bank account, and until you set it up you'll be waiting on paper checks; enroll the week you get Axess access
Direct deposit step 1: Go to Axess
Direct deposit step 2: From the Student role, open the My Finances tab and select Direct Deposit
Direct deposit step 3: Add your account — routing number (usually 9 digits) and account number (usually 10–12 digits, not a card number), type = checking or savings
Direct deposit step 4: Set Deposit Type to percent, Amount to 100, Deposit Order to 1 — set up only one account; the multiple-account option causes failed deposits
Direct deposit step 5: Verify and submit; if in doubt, confirm the numbers with your bank

Stanford Federal Credit Union (SFCU) — branches at Tresidder Union (2nd floor) and near EV; unusually friendly to students with no US credit history — immediate debit card and a guaranteed credit card even without an SSN or US income (bring passport, proof of address, and student ID); go in person
Chase — 855 El Camino Real
Bank of America — 3000 El Camino Real, near Cal Ave; ATM on campus at Tresidder
Citibank — 250 University Ave, historically willing to issue student cards without credit history and convenient if already a Citi client at home
Wells Fargo — Tresidder, 2nd floor

Trade-offs are the usual: campus convenience and ATM access versus national footprint; cheap accounts versus willingness to issue no-history credit cards. The MyGSB banking page has the current lay of the land

US payments culture: cards for everything (even coffee); Venmo dominates student-to-student payments (expect a ~$300 weekly limit until identity verified and bank linked), though many keep Zelle too; person-to-person bank transfers otherwise rare; a checkbook still matters for off-campus rent; gas pumps and some online stores refuse foreign cards — a US debit card solves it

Taxes: fellowship and stipend income can be taxable, summer internship income certainly is, and California has its own filing; free help exists (IRS VITA sites, campus workshops each spring); international students have special non-resident rules; keep award letters and pay stubs in one folder from day one
The premium-card debate (Amex Platinum vs. Chase Sapphire Reserve vs. Capital One Venture X) ran for months among classmates

Rough bucketing: Chase is strongest for hotels (Hyatt transfers), Amex for aspirational flights (business/first-class redemptions) and Centurion lounges, and Venture X for a lower-effort break-even; Amex's fee is easier to offset with credits, but it depends on travel style

Sign-up bonuses are where the real value is; if you play the points game you'll eventually rotate through all the premium cards for their bonuses — start with Chase, because their 5/24-style rule rejects applicants who've opened more than five cards in the last two years
Small perk: Walmart+ membership comes free with Amex Platinum — useful for grocery delivery
New to US credit (internationals, but also anyone thin-filed): start building immediately — scores take years and landlords check them the week you graduate; paths in Chapter 21
You can pay the rent portion of GSB housing charges through the Bilt app's “Pay Rent” tab, which generates the account and routing numbers the school needs — earning points at no fee
Each quarter you can opt out of the ASSU student-activities fee if you don't use the graduate clubs it funds — typically ~$50 back per quarter via the waiver form; windows are short
Paid tuition late? You can raise a support ticket to waive a tuition late fee — once, ever; save the mulligan for when it matters

Get a US number working before Week Zero — you will meet hundreds of people, and every list, group chat, delivery, and two-factor prompt needs a US number; carrier stores cluster on University Avenue and El Camino Real near California Avenue
Coverage on campus: AT&T and Verizon are historically strongest; T-Mobile is fine but patchy in some corners and basements; check the signal in your actual room before committing

Field reports: T-Mobile produced “no service at all most of the time” in a Schwab couples suite — calls to employers and investors dropping mid-sentence; Mint Mobile was near-unusable inside JMac rooms and patchy in the GSB itself (fine outdoors); AT&T covered everywhere tested. Turn on Wi-Fi calling and the dead zones mostly stop mattering

Three national networks: Verizon (the traditional “premium” network), AT&T (vies for the top slot; historically the internationals' favorite because it didn't demand SSNs), and T-Mobile (cheapest unlimited plans, weakest in fringe spots)

MVNOs (Mint Mobile, Google Fi, Cricket, and dozens more) resell the big networks' towers under cheaper brands; Mint Mobile supports Wi-Fi calling and text; MVNO SIMs can be ordered online and even shipped to a friend before you arrive

Postpaid is a monthly contract billed in arrears, with roaming/overage extras and device financing on top; prepaid is all-inclusive at the sticker price (“a $50 plan costs $50”), usually with free or cheap international calling but no roaming abroad. Verdict: prepaid wins on cost and switching flexibility; postpaid wins on roaming and customer service

Family plans — 2–5 lines on one account at roughly $30–$60 per member — are the classic hack: join an American classmate's plan or form one with other students. Number portability between carriers is easy once you're off contract
One warning worth repeating: paying a phone bill does not build US credit — carriers only report late payments
Condensed from the International Student Handbook's US-carrier primer, updated for the post-Sprint era
Check the Stanford mobile discounts page before signing anything — AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon have all offered Stanford rates
Checklist item 1: Read the Admit tab of MyGSB end to end, and watch the MyGSB Digest emails over the summer — official deadlines flow through them
Checklist item 2: Decide on Cardinal Care vs. waiver (Chapter 4) before the mid-September deadline; internationals confirm your alternative plan is waiver-eligible first
Checklist item 3: Clear Stanford's immunization requirements through Vaden — MMR, the Hepatitis B series plus antibody titer, and TB screening — and bring your records (translated if needed)
Checklist item 4: Book flights to arrive comfortably before Week Zero; line up first-night housing if your contract starts later
Checklist item 5: Ship or order room basics; confirm your residence's package policy; pack one set of linens
Checklist item 6: Set up direct deposit on Axess; open a US bank account plan (internationals: read Chapter 21 first)
Checklist item 7: Sort a US phone plan, or a plan to get one in week one
Checklist item 8: Submit your ID-card photo online in advance to skip the Tresidder line

Pact Rule — No Early Action: Hosts Don't Tour, Show, or Soft-Commit a Passdown Before January 1; MBA1 Groups Don't Pressure Them for Early Access; Early Outreach Gets a Friendly Note Pointing to the Pact and Timeline
Pact Rule — Equal Access After the Date: From January 1, Hosts Give Reasonable, Good-Faith Access to Every Interested Group and Communicate Their Process and Timeline Clearly
Pact Is a Norm, Not a Contract — No Penalties, Just a Meaningfully Saner Housing Market for the Class That Comes After You

Second Year Runs on a Different Scarcity: as an MBA1 the Constraint Was Information; as an MBA2 It's Intention
Housing Renewal Mostly Works — Students Who Held Their Lease Through the Summer Generally Renewed the Same Unit; Nobody Who Wanted to Stay in the Midrises Was Known to Be Forced Out
Group Housing Applications: Everyone Applies, One Leader Forms the Group, and the Group Rides the Leader's Priority
Housing Selection Runs Late April/Early May
MBA2s Register First Each Quarter — the Classes You Missed as an MBA1 Are Suddenly Gettable
Plan Your Remaining Requirements (Units, the Last Core/Foundations Boxes) at the Start of the Year, Not the End
Build the Year Backward From Super Round — the One or Two Classes Locked in Spring (Chapter 13) Are the Anchors; Arrange the Rest of the Schedule Around Them
Spend Your Across-the-Street Ambitions — If the d.school Studio, the Law Seminar, or the Engineering Class Has Been 'Someday' Since Fall of MBA1, This Is the Someday
Front-Load Fall and Winter — Dis-O, the Last Treks, and the Goodbyes All Land in Spring, So Many MBA2s Deliberately Keep Spring Light
If You Interned, the Return-Offer Decision Dominates Early Fall of MBA2 Year
Extension Asks Are Routine in Most Industries — the CMC (Chapter 14) Knows What's Normal in Yours and Has Seen Every Version of This Conversation
Decide What You'd Do With a 'No' Before You Ask for an Extension
Full-Time Recruiting Is a Different Animal — Fewer Structured Pipelines, More Just-in-Time Postings, and Far More Weight on Direct Outreach
Changing Lanes Late Is Common — Just-in-Time Roles Cluster Near Graduation by Definition, and Every Class Has People Who Signed in Spring, Plenty Glad They Held Out
Becoming the Infrastructure: the Peer Mentors, Blast Admins, Guide-Writers, and Chat-Founders of Your MBA2 Year Are What Made Your MBA1 Year Work — It's All Volunteers
Arbuckle Fellows (Coaching the Next Year's Leadership Labs Squads) Take Applications in MBA1 Spring
Structured Peer-Mentor Programs Take Applications in MBA1 Spring — Watch the Digest, Because by Fall Those Doors Are Closed

Leave the Passdowns Better Than You Found Them — the Highest-Leverage Hour of MBA2 Spring Is the One Spent Updating the Version the Next Class Inherits
The Social Geometry Changes When the Class Below Arrives — You're the Older Class Now, the One With the Answers, the Apartment, and the June Furniture to Sell
Professor Relationships Have an Expiration Date — Office Hours Cost Nothing Now and Are Unrecoverable in July
The Advice That Echoed: Take the Across-the-Street Class That Intimidates You, Spend Real Time With MSx Students and the Class Below, and Leave Space to Show Up for Each Other
The Week Zero Letter (Chapter 22) Gets Opened at Dis-O — If You Never Wrote One, Write It in Fall; Late Is Fine, the Point Is the Distance

Alumni Email Account 2: the GSB Alumni Address (Also Google-Hosted)

Step 2: at the Stanford Forwarding Page, Point Your SUNet Mail at sunet@alumni.stanford.edu (Used Over the Longer, Typo-Prone GSB Address) and Select 'Do NOT Keep a Copy' or You'll Get Duplicates

Step 3: Inside the GSB Alumni Gmail's Forwarding Settings, Add sunet@alumni.stanford.edu as a Forwarding Address — if Google's Verification Keeps Erroring, Sign Into the Alumni Account in Your Phone's Mail App First to Unstick It
Step 4: After a Few Days of Confirmed Flow, Sign Out of the Old Account for Good and Send Yourself a Hello-World
Forwarding From Your Old Address Lasts About Two Years
Your Stanford Google Account Survives Roughly 3 Months After Graduation (Longer if You're International) — Export Everything With Google Takeout Well Before It Lapses
Update Accounts Registered to Your Stanford Email Before It Dies; Alumni Keep Some Library and Career Resources — Check the Alumni-Relations Page for the Current List

Your @stanford.edu Stops Working a Few Months After Graduation

Dis-Orientation (Dis-O): the Roughly Two Weeks Before Graduation — a Student-Run Festival of Last Lectures From Nominated Professors, LP Parties, Day Trips, Farm-to-Table Dinners, Party Buses to the City, a Bollywood Send-Off, and a Final 'TALK Epilogue'
Single Most Important Logistical Lesson: Do Not Schedule Travel in the Days Before Graduation — the People Who Did Regretted Missing Dis-O
Within Dis-O, Last Lecture Asks a Few Beloved Professors to Give the Talk They'd Give if It Were the Last Thing They Could Teach You — Those Become the Lines the Class Quotes for Weeks
Quote: "One day we are going to look back on this time and wish we were still living in it." — Graham Weaver, in a Last Lecture
Grad Photos With the Red Stole Happen Weeks Before June — the Stanford Bookstore Stocks Stoles Starting Around April, in a Surprising Range of Colors and Styles
Best Grad-Photo Window Is Mid-May — Waiting for the June Weeks Risks Every Group on Campus Queuing at Hoover Tower and Memorial Church With the Same Plan
The Classmate-Photographer Market Is Also Excellent and Cheap
The Flight-Home Ritual: Before You Land After Graduation, Write Something — a Diary Entry, a Reflection — Capture What These Years Meant Before Ordinary Life Crowds It Out; Take the Two Hours

Move-Out: Re-Read the End of Chapter 9 (Command Hooks, Inventory Photos, Inspection List)
Sell Through #all_buy_sell and SU Post — the June Buyer's Market Is the September Seller's Market Inverted

nodes.label: Chapter 7 Cheat Sheet closing bullets (weekly rhythm, academics, careers, cross the street, health, trips)
Join the channels on day one: Blast (from your original SUNet address), the class WhatsApp, Slack, or you'll miss the school's real bulletin board (Chapter 12)
The weekly rhythm: FOAM Tuesdays, TALKs Wednesdays, BPL Thursdays, LPF Fridays, and Town Square every day 11:30-1:15 (Chapter 15)
Academics tip: take the level you'll actually learn in; grades are nondisclosure; the registration lottery rewards people who read Chapter 13 once, carefully
Careers tip: your @stanford.edu email is a superpower - founders and executives reply; start outreach before you feel ready (Chapter 14)
Cross the street: a huge share of what's special at Stanford lives outside the GSB - classes, institutes, libraries, makerspaces (Chapters 8 and 13)
Health tip: start at Vaden - Cardinal Care enforces referrals (Chapter 4); bikes are the default transport, free loaner helmets live at Schwab (Chapter 9)
Trips tip: the GST lottery, Vegas FOAM, and Tahoe weekends are the calendar anchors - watch the deadlines (Chapters 15 and 16)

nodes.label: Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Remember that maybe a tenth of what's remarkable at Stanford lives at the GSB - a starter set of the rest, all a few minutes bike ride from where you sleep
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Dish: a 3.7-mile loop through the foothills past a 150-foot radio telescope built in 1961 - a Cold-War instrument that later talked to the Voyager spacecraft and still operates; sunrise or sunset is the move, no bikes on the loop; the signature Stanford side quest (dish.stanford.edu)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Cantor Arts Center is free and holds one of the largest collections of Rodin bronzes outside Paris, including a cast of The Gates of Hell; the outdoor sculpture garden is open 24/7 (museum.stanford.edu)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Next door, the Anderson Collection (also free; Thursday-Monday 11-5, no reservation) is a jaw-dropping room of postwar American art - Rothko, de Kooning, and Pollock's Lucifer
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Papua New Guinea Sculpture Garden: a true deep cut, sixty-plus works carved on-site in 1994 by master carvers brought from the Sepik River; free tours run the fourth Sunday of each month
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Nearby, the 1880s Arizona Cactus Garden is a quiet, photogenic place to reset
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Hoover Tower's 250-foot observation deck (free for Stanford affiliates; bring binoculars) sees San Francisco on a clear day
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Windhover is a free contemplative center built around Nathan Oliveira's paintings, with an outdoor labyrinth - the campus's best-kept quiet spot
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Big science you can actually visit: SLAC, the two-mile linear accelerator (the longest in the world until 2017, and the source of six Nobel Prizes), runs free ninety-minute public tours a couple of times a month - register ahead
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Coffee House ('the CoHo') has been the student living room since 1966 - coffee, beer, open mics
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Memorial Church and the sandstone Main Quad are the architectural heart of campus
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Tradition to catch: Full Moon on the Quad (October)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Tradition to catch: fountain hopping - there's an unofficial ranking, and President Levin admits he did it
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Tradition to catch: Primal Scream (midnight screaming during dead week)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Tradition to catch: the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band (LSJUMB) - the 'band' that scatters instead of marching and has been fined by the NCAA and banned from Disneyland (Stanford magazine)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Make something with your hands: the Product Realization Lab (PRL) is a hands-on fabrication and manufacturing shop open to students through its courses
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: ME 203, Design and Fabrication, teaches you to actually run the mill, the lathe, and the rest of real on-the-ground manufacturing
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: making.stanford.edu indexes every campus shop and studio - welding, woodworking, laser-cutting, 3D printing - most with open hours and quarter-long classes
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The LOFT is a graduate design studio worth getting a friend to walk you into
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Stanford educational farm: for the opposite of a machine shop, classes in regenerative agriculture where an afternoon's 'work' is harvesting snap peas - sometimes literally touching grass is the whole point
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: CCRMA (say 'karma'), the Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics, up at The Knoll, is where music meets code - synthesis, spatial audio, and the Stanford Laptop Orchestra (SLOrk); runs a concert series of new computer music, join the mailing list; open courses like Music 101
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Stanford Bookstore: the official four-floor campus store, with the Cardinal Technology Center - Stanford apparel and gifts on the main floor, faculty-authored books and a cafe upstairs, textbooks and supplies in the basement, computers and software (often at education pricing) at the tech center
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Stanford Live: the university's professional performing-arts presenter, at Bing Concert Hall and the open-air Frost Amphitheater; students get deeply discounted tickets (usually two per show with your ID), free masterclasses, and artist talks
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Continuing Studies: open-enrollment evening and online courses - liberal arts, creative writing, wellness, professional skills - that anyone can take with no application; a low-key way for you, a partner, or family to take a Stanford class purely for the joy of it
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Field stations, if you wander: Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve, 1,200 acres of protected foothills open by docent-led tour
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Field stations, if you wander: Hopkins Marine Station, Stanford's 1892 marine lab next door to the Monterey Bay Aquarium
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Stanford Theatre: off campus but essential - a lovingly restored 1925 movie palace on University Avenue (funded by the Packard family) that screens Hollywood classics from 1910-1970 on 35mm, with a live Wurlitzer organ between shows; a perfect low-cost date night
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The McMurtry Building: the home of Art & Art History, right beside the Cantor and the Anderson - a striking Diller Scofidio + Renfro building (2015) with art studios, film and media labs, the Bowes Art & Architecture Library, and ground-floor galleries and a roof garden open to visitors
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: The Red Barn: Stanford's historic horse barn, out toward the foothills, home to the Stanford Riding Academy - English and western riding lessons open to students, staff, and community on a quarterly schedule (there's even a for-credit wellness version)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Bing Nursery School: Stanford's laboratory preschool in the southeast corner of campus, which doubles as a child-development research site (the famous 'marshmallow test' ran here); play-based, half-day sessions from age two to kindergarten, competitive to get into so ask early
nodes.source_location: Chapter 8: Getting Oriented - Deep cuts: the Stanford side quests

nodes.label: Frost, in festival mode: beyond the professional Stanford Live shows, the amphitheater hosts two beloved student-run festivals - the end-of-year Frost Music & Arts Festival (run by the student Stanford Concert Network) and Blackfest, a celebration of Black art and community - both with real touring headliners

nodes.label: Schwab field guide
Schwab has a small gym, rental bikes for JMac and Schwab residents (a good way to start before buying your own), and large red moving bins you can check out from the front desk
Know this: the Schwab front desk is the front desk for both Schwab and Jack McDonald - whatever you need, that's the counter
The Schwab front desk is staffed 24/7 - the fallback for lockouts, dead door batteries, and stranded deliveries
Free loaner helmets live in the Schwab entryway cupboard - no bike rental required, guests included
Warning: use one even for the two-minute hops - one classmate was cut off riding just from the GSB to Schwab, fell, and hit her head

You can order room, bathroom, or kitchen cleanings through the front desk anytime. The standard service covers: dusting and wipe-downs of surfaces, baseboards, doors and frames; mirrors and interior windows; sweeping, vacuuming, and mopping; bedsheet changes if fresh sheets are left out; trash in cans; shower, sink, and toilet sanitizing; kitchen counters, range tops, microwave, stove and oven, the exterior of the fridge, and whatever dishes fit in the sink
Not covered: excessive dish mountains, moving lots of personal items, or the inside of the fridge

Housekeeping, priced: services run Tuesdays and Thursdays, 8 a.m.-4 p.m. (last appointment 3 p.m.): roughly $75 for bed and bath (an hour), $150 adding the kitchen (two hours), $225 for a whole couple suite (three hours)
After ten paid services the eleventh is free, and recurring weekly, biweekly, or monthly schedules can be set up at the front desk. Book about a week ahead - slots go
Dry cleaning: PurpleTie
The PurpleTie drop-off/pickup locker is in the JMac lower lobby (room 015), with pickup and delivery every weekday evening 4-7 p.m. and next-business-evening standard turnaround
Setup: sign up for @HOME service at purpletie.com/sign-up - choose zip 94305, Address Line 1 '650 Jane Stanford Way,' Address Line 2 'Jack McDonald Hall,' with a US mobile number for delivery texts
Process: grab a bag from the closet shelf, fill out an order form, drop it in the closet before 4 p.m. (11:30 a.m. deadline for same-evening pickup)
Questions: 1 (855) PURPLETIE
Keys, lockouts, and access
After-hours maintenance emergencies (all R&DE housing): (650) 725-1602
In the GSB Residences, a key that stops working usually means the door's battery died - the 24/7 Schwab desk fixes it
In EVGR, card readers can be temperamental - try three or four times before giving up

GSB students not living in the Residences can request card access: Facilities Operations, Charlie Munger Building room CM004 (the basement office by the lost and found). EVGR residents wanting JMac/Schwab access use the office at the basement stairs to the right of Arbuckle dining
Mail, packages, and deliveries

JMac's street address is 650 Jane Stanford Way; Schwab is 680. For groceries and food deliveries, many JMac residents route to the Schwab desk (680) anyway - drivers find it more easily and the desk holds food for hours
Returns: don't fight the 'schedule a pickup' flow. Choose the drop-off option, print the label, and leave the package on the carrier shelf (UPS, USPS, FedEx) in the mail room

In non-GSB housing, private carriers sometimes can't access buildings and hallway packages get stolen - register with the Graduate Housing Package Center to auto-forward packages to your front desk (International Student Handbook)
Anything broken in your unit - creaky doors, clogged drains, failing appliances, electrical - file a Fix-It request; a technician comes within days and it's included in your housing bill

Streaming devices (Apple TV, Chromecast) are fussy on shared university networks - your building's Resident Computer Consultants (RCCs), paid student tech support, exist for exactly this. Or run your own router (Chapter 11)

nodes.label: Wi-Fi that actually works

Campus networks: Stanford (register your devices), Stanford Visitor (day-one stopgap, low bandwidth), eduroam (works at universities worldwide with your Stanford login). Register every device at rnt.stanford.edu; the network-registration guide covers the odd cases, including how to declare a device someone else (e.g., a partner) primarily uses

The router upgrade (the single most-thanked tech tip of the year): get an ethernet cable from your front desk, plug into your room's wired port (it's the landline telephone port in GSB residences), register your router's MAC address at rnt.stanford.edu, and enjoy your own fast, no-login Wi-Fi network that every smart device connects to painlessly
The budget pick that works with Stanford's system: TP-Link AX1800 WiFi 6 (V4) - Amazon link

Smart-home fix, Google Home: find the MAC address in the Home app (device -> settings -> device info), register it at rnt.stanford.edu, wait 30 minutes, then connect phone and speaker to Stanford Wi-Fi; if the speaker was never set up, first pair phone+speaker on any network (a friend's hotspot works)
HomePods work after a factory reset and repair through the Home app
Amazon Echo - if MAC registration isn't enough, factory-reset the device; IT couldn't crack this one, a classmate did
IT support
Walk-up IT desk: Bass Center level 2, in the corner by the staircases (elevator side) - historically room B207, Mon/Tue/Thu/Fri 10-12:30 and 2:30-5. Phone: 650-725-HELP
GSB tech contact page: here; appointments: crctime.stanford.edu/gsb450nsite; knowledge base: services.stanford.edu; Lathrop tech center: thehub.stanford.edu

During Week Zero, book the IT-setup appointment offered in the Digest - a technician configures Wi-Fi and printing on all your devices, and setup is harder than it looks (International Student Handbook)

nodes.label: Printing

How it works: log in at the Cardinal Print portal with your SUNet ID, upload documents, then tap your ID on any campus printer and hit 'print release.' You can also email attachments to Cardinalprint@stanford.edu from your Stanford address. No account setup needed; your GSB print allotment is generous enough that almost nobody exhausts it, and it barely matters which account you bill
Caveat: if nothing happens after you hit print, it's file size - under ~2 MB is instant, bigger files need a wait
'Insufficient Funds' over the summer? Pick the other payment option - it bills your student account via Axess. Working printers live in JMac, EVGR, and Bass

The allotment, precisely: the GSB allocates $100 per student per year for Cardinal Print. Select the GSB account code when releasing a job (the printer screen lists it) or the default silently bills your student account instead

Photo and cardstock printing: CVS at Town & Country for same-day photos; FedEx print centers on Cal Ave and El Camino (Menlo Park) for nicer stock; Shutterfly mails cheap prints if quality isn't critical

Free from Stanford: Microsoft Office
Free from Stanford: Zoom Pro - log in via SSO at stanford.zoom.us, type your stanford.edu address, don't use the Google button
Free from Stanford: Dashlane password manager, MATLAB and other academic software, Qualtrics, VPN, LinkedIn Learning, Coursera
Free from Stanford: live TV via Puffer (NBC, CBS, ABC, PBS, Fox, CW)

The original linked list is also preserved as Free Software List.docx in the Resources folder - original list via Charlie Michael, expanded with the class's additions

The AI accounts Stanford gives you
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: As of June 30, 2026, Stanford has an enterprise education agreement with OpenAI, and every active student gets an account - ignore old workarounds about bolting a personal ChatGPT account onto your Stanford email. It is part of a campus AI pilot running through August 2027, so assume the details will move (Stanford UIT's ChatGPT Edu page)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: Use it with eyes open: your chat history and personal context live on an account tied to your Stanford identity, and historically migrating an account's history out when you graduate has been painful to impossible. Keep long-running projects and anything you'd hate to lose on a personal account, and treat the Stanford-provided AI as at-your-own-risk convenience
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: ChatGPT Edu (Standard) - free with an active SUNet ID. You get higher message limits than the free tier, data analysis, web browsing, document summarization, Codex for coding help, and the ability to build custom GPTs. Request it through the UIT service page. There is also a Pro tier, but it needs a funding source (a PTA)
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: Claude for Education and Gemini Enterprise - Stanford runs the same arrangement with Anthropic and Google, so you can pick the model you actually like rather than paying for three subscriptions
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: The AI Playground - Stanford's own sandbox for trying models side by side, with an AI API gateway if you're building something
nodes.source_location: Chapter 11 - The AI accounts Stanford gives you

nodes.label: Why to use the Stanford account: ChatGPT Edu is approved for low-, moderate-, and high-risk data (including PHI), your conversations aren't used to train OpenAI's models, and it carries extra copyright protections. The consumer version gives you none of that - and it largely supersedes the ChatGPT student discount, so check before you pay for anything

nodes.label: The student-discount playbook
Verify once through SheerID - the service most companies use to check student status; it then unlocks a whole class of offers automatically
The big automated ones: two free months of ChatGPT Plus, Spotify Premium Student, Superhuman's education plan (about $10 a month instead of $30), and Fantastical at 20% off

Just ask: most smaller AI and productivity tools grant an education discount if you email their support with your Stanford address (classmates have had Granola's limits lifted and cut rates on transcription and writing tools this way)
Caveat: deals change constantly, so always check the current offer

nodes.label: The Blast FAQ, distilled

Who runs it: the Student Association Campus Life Committee sets up the lists (on Stanford servers) and appoints the 'Blast Sheriff.' Nobody reviews messages for content or accuracy - it's yours, collectively. Membership is entirely optional
Mind your language: a Stanford-wide spam filter the Sheriffs can't control eats vulgarity

Subscribing: sign up from your original SUNet email (not an alias, not Gmail) via your class's list page, then email the Sheriffs (gsb-blast-all-owner@lists.stanford.edu) to expedite approval - they get many non-GSB requests. Watch for the confirmation email in spam

Blast-All is an alias, not a separate list - if you're on your class list, you're getting everything. Digest mode exists but isn't recommended (you'll miss time-sensitive posts); filter into a label instead
Finding old posts: every successful Blast lands in your class list's public Archive page - search there before asking 'did anyone see that email about...'

Caveat: joint-degree students (JD/MBA, EIPER, and friends) graduating with a later class must re-subscribe to that class's list themselves - nothing moves automatically. And Blasts only send from the exact @stanford.edu address that joined the list
The Blast Tax

In 2008 a second-year named Amal Dorai, drowning in some fifty blasts a day, sent a half-joking email calculating that each all-school blast cost the community about $54 of 'expected utility' - and proposed that anyone sending one should 'pay it back' by adding something genuinely funny or interesting at the end

He meant it as a joke; the first-years took it as law, and it stuck. To this day a blast without a worthwhile nugget at the bottom invites a gentle pile-on, and a volunteer 'Blast Sheriff' informally enforces the norm (Business Insider, 'Codebreaker')

It has not reduced the volume of email one bit - but it has made the class funnier. And the tax has a quieter function, the FAQ notes: it makes you pause and ask whether Blast is the right forum at all

WhatsApp

WhatsApp is where the real-time life of the class happens. Each class builds its own ecosystem - an everyone chat, an All Academics chat, an events/parties chat, buy/sell chats, a free-food group, interest and club chats, and an internationals group bridged with the year above
Join WhatsApp groups early and liberally; mute liberally too

A class contact directory model from the class of 2026: name + WhatsApp + more, collected by form and exported as importable .vcf contact cards, on a give-to-get basis. It hit ~90% participation and made the class feel navigable overnight. (Collect dietary preferences in the form - it pays off at every dinner for two years.)

The form fields that made the directory work: first and last name; WhatsApp number in strict +countrycode, digits-only format (malformed numbers break the .vcf export); an optional non-WhatsApp number; Stanford and personal emails; LinkedIn and Instagram URLs; workplaces in comma'd order; Venmo handle; home city and country; schools attended; birthday; campus housing and room number; interests; and non-English languages spoken
One data-handling note for the builder: keep access limited to contributors, and think twice before collecting room numbers in any exportable sheet
An advice-sharing WhatsApp group where MBA2s answer anything - the group this guide is largely mined from. Someone in your class should start one in week one

nodes.label: Take the level you're actually going to learn in — no glory for all-advanced classes, no shame for all-base; no one cares or asks

Accelerated-finance format: readings expected done before class (deliberately flipped); live, time-boxed partner exercises for a grade — valuable pressure for some, stress that hampers learning for others
Self-test for accelerated finance from a classmate who loved it: "if you can't teach yourself from a textbook, don't take it"
Do the weekly mini-projects early and think them through deeply — they're where the learning is
FIN 207 (after base finance) drew a strong review from a "quintuple-base baddie": a helpful corporations-and-governance overview taught by a good professor duo who coldcall knowing your background
If GSB finance electives lock you out entirely, Corporate Financial Management (MS&E 249) across the street "made a lot click" for one classmate — light lift, great lectures
Level-switch forms are released on a schedule early in fall, found in Canvas under the autumn "analytic foundations" module
Practical study tactic for the quantitative cores: do every homework problem properly, and keep solutions templatized in a spreadsheet you can reference — Celeste Bean
Excel vs. Google Sheets: most coursework can be done in Sheets, but real Excel is needed for data tables/sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo work in the modeling cores
The fall "Train the Street"-style Excel workshops are worth the two hours (follow-along spreadsheets included)
Course-required online textbooks/software (MyLab and kin) usually can't be bought separately from the digital textbook — budget for it (~$130 in recent years, with two-year access)

AI and the honor code: every syllabus sets its own AI policy — from "use anything, cite it" to "closed-book everything"; check before using AI on anything graded, and ask in week one when the syllabus is silent

nodes.label: GSBGEN 390: an individual research project with a faculty sponsor; MBA1s can take it starting spring quarter, a separate process from elective registration

Your 390 sponsor must be current GSB faculty (lecturers only if teaching at the GSB that quarter — check the faculty directory)

Your 390 petition is essentially a project overview: a precise research question and knowledge gap, background, success criteria, and a defined deliverable (paper, white paper, data model, toolkit, memo, or presentation)
Share a v1 draft with prospective 390 sponsors to make saying yes easy, and follow up with a deadline

390 fine print: MBA2s can file any quarter; MBA1s spring only, with a minimum 3.0 GPA; MSx students after their first quarter; projects must be academic in nature, not credit for a job, internship, or your own startup

nodes.label: The Byers Center for Biodesign (recently renamed the Mussallem Center), based in the medical school — the crown jewel for health care/medtech

Biodesign's founding process: Identify a real clinical need (fellows embed in hospitals, collect hundreds of unmet needs before inventing anything), Invent (prototype fast, kill bad ideas early), and Implement (map the regulatory, reimbursement, and funding path)
Biodesign's flagship ten-month Innovation Fellowship deliberately mixes MBAs with engineers, clinicians, and designers
Biodesign-born technologies have launched roughly sixty health companies (including iRhythm) and reached tens of millions of patients
Biodesign website: biodesign.stanford.edu
There's a full Biodesign course sequence open to enrolled students if you want the method without the fellowship

HAI — the Institute for Human-Centered AI (founded 2019, and as of 2026 merged with Stanford's data-science effort): works on AI's technology, policy, and human impact; its conferences draw the field's biggest names
Bio-X — Stanford's original interdisciplinary biosciences institute (1998, in the Clark Center), where biologists, engineers, clinicians, and physicists collide on problems in biology and medicine
The Woods Institute for the Environment — the university's environmental-research hub (within the Doerr School of Sustainability), spanning faculty across all seven schools
The Precourt Institute for Energy — Stanford's energy-research hub (also within the Doerr School of Sustainability), best known for the long-running weekly Energy Seminar, open to anyone
SIEPR — the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (1982), a nonpartisan bridge between economists and business, tech, and government leaders; its public lectures are excellent

FSI — the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, housed in Encina Hall a short walk from the GSB Residences; spans CISAC, CDDRL, and the Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center, with a near-constant calendar of public talks

The Hoover Institution — the public-policy think tank at the base of Hoover Tower (founded 1919 by Herbert Hoover; leans right-of-center, runs events almost daily); its Library & Archives holds roughly a million volumes and six thousand collections from 171 countries; tower galleries are free and open daily, with free exhibition tours on Thursdays

CASBS — the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, the residential think tank on the hill above campus (founded 1954), where behavioral economics largely took shape when Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky were in residence

The Stanford Humanities Center — since 1980, the university's hub for humanities research, home to some forty fellows a year and a full calendar of public lectures, seminars, and workshops open to anyone

The Haas Center for Public Service — Stanford's home for service since 1985; its Cardinal Quarter program places students in full-time quarter- or summer-long roles with nonprofits and government agencies (five hundred-plus options a year), with training and funding attached

PACS — the Center on Philanthropy and Civil Society, home of the Stanford Social Innovation Review: the university's hub for philanthropy, nonprofits, and civil-society research, with fellowships and events of its own
Stanford maintains a directory of every independent lab, center, and institute

Institutes are far more open than they look — some of the best relationships at Stanford come from simply emailing people at institutes like FSI and Hoover and asking to talk; faculty, fellows, and staff are often remarkably receptive to a curious student

Action Learning Program (ALP) — project-based electives where a team solves a real, current problem for a partner organization (Product Management, Digital Marketing, The Founder's Right Hand, the Public Policy Labs, and more)

Design courses: DESIGN 235 View from the Future, DESIGN 262 Design for Healthy Behaviors, DESIGN 261 Systems Design for Health, ENGR 104B Designing Your Life (mixed reviews — "read the book instead")
Wellness courses: WELLNESS 123 Living on Purpose, 183 Financial Wellness, 130 Meditation, 107A Behavior Design (Fogg), 108 Leadership from Within, PSYC 233 Mindfulness in Medicine
Worth checking: BIOS 237 Wearables, CHPR 242 Science of Well-being, CS 342 Building for Digital Health, EPI 219, MED 229 Longevity, MED 213 Digital Future of Health Care, PSYCH 234, PSYCH 262
There's also a spreadsheet of Stanford's healthcare institutes
Email-finding tools: Apollo.io and Hunter.io free tiers are the CMC-endorsed options (no Stanford-upgraded plans exist)
SPIRE (Stanford Professionals in Real Estate) — the real estate community lives outside the classroom

nodes.source_location: Careers — Track-Specific Resource Packs: Real Estate

nodes.label: The Golden Shovel — the annual Stanford–Berkeley development competition
nodes.source_location: Careers — Track-Specific Resource Packs: Real Estate

nodes.label: In the classroom, the anchor figures are practitioner-professors Chris Mahowald and Doug Abbey — their courses are the spine of the real estate track
nodes.source_location: Careers — Track-Specific Resource Packs: Real Estate

nodes.label: SPIRE maintains a full list of real-estate courses across Stanford
nodes.source_location: Careers — Track-Specific Resource Packs: Real Estate

nodes.label: Jackson Library stocks the three ULI development textbooks: Miles et al., Real Estate Development; Schmitz & Brett, Market Analysis; Peiser & Frej, Professional Real Estate Development
nodes.source_location: Careers — Track-Specific Resource Packs: Real Estate

nodes.label: Workshops & drop-ins: fall workshops on classroom participation and impromptu speaking; Vocal Yoga, a weekly drop-in lunch on voice and projection
LOWKeynotes: the TED-style program that selects ~30 students a year, pairing classroom workshops with small-group and 1:1 coaching (budget 6–15 hours/week near the end — worth it)

Coaching: a Communications Coaching Program with an assigned coach in autumn and a coach marketplace after; plus the Hume Center for Writing and Speaking and the Stanford Language Center across the street, and the Think Fast, Talk Smart podcast as homework

Nikhil Jain's take: Strategic Communication and Winning Writing were both worth it — one presentation style per week (improv, long-form, persuasion, Q&A) in the former; a piece of writing per week with real feedback in the latter; "it's useless to be getting feedback on ChatGPT B-minus content"
General podcasts: Acquired, Think Fast Talk Smart
Media & consumer podcasts: The Ankler, The Town with Matthew Belloni, Modern Retail, On Production
Tech & VC podcasts: 20VC, BG2Pod, This Week in Startups, Open Source with Amanda Robson, Lenny's Podcast

The course ladder: Startup Garage (the canonical startup class), Lean Launchpad (rigorously test an idea), Launchpad (actually build and ship), Formation of New Ventures (case-based — more discussion than build, learn from founders)

The sector-specific builders: Hacking for Climate, Hacking for Defense, Venture Creation for the Real Economy, Stanford Climate Ventures, Biodesign (and Biodesign for Digital Health), and Design for Extreme Affordability — pick the one aimed at your industry for the build experience plus the sector's network
Choosing between the builders: Lean Launchpad runs 15–20 hours a week and grants across-the-street rather than GSB credits; Startup Garage carries GSB credits — go in committed either way
Stanford Venture Studio — the GSB's founder co-working and support space; sign up, all are welcome
Cardinal Ventures and the Emergence Student Accelerator add university-wide accelerator options
BBLs (brown-bag lunches) with founders and investors happen nearly daily — "an embarrassment of options"
Emergence, briefly: health-impact focus (food security, housing, education, healthcare access all qualify), open to every discipline; applications close in late November for a winter-quarter program
Startup Garage and friends hold regular office hours; the Stanford Lab Registry helps you find research labs to partner with

More ecosystem: the Stanford Entrepreneurship Network indexes everything startup-flavored across the university; the Venture Formation Lab has an intake form; the Entrepreneurial Summer Program (ESP) funds full-time summer startup work; and an advisor-shared Airtable compares every "design and build your own thing" class
The hub is the Stanford Venture Studio (SVS) — the CoLab co-working space in M101, plus a program run by the Grousbeck-Holloway Center
Startup Office Hours — most weeks, a free one-on-one with a rotating cast of VCs, founders, startup lawyers (Cooley, DLA Piper, Wilson Sonsini), and even a startup-immigration attorney
VC 101 and Legal 101 — recurring explainer sessions on how venture and startup law actually work, plus small "Startup Umbrella Grant" micro-grants to get moving
The weekly SVS newsletter carries every entrepreneurship deadline on campus, and there's an annual Demo Day

Startup Garage and Lean Launchpad — the two flagship courses (the multi-quarter build-a-company sequence, and Steve Blank's customer-discovery method); together, you can go from idea to funded pilot without leaving campus

The search fund — "entrepreneurship through acquisition": the idea was conceived at the GSB in 1984; raise a small fund from a dozen-odd investors to spend up to two years searching for one good small business to buy, then raise acquisition capital, buy it, and run it as CEO
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Search Fund: Stanford's Signature Entrepreneurial Path

nodes.label: The school's Search Fund Primer (from the Grousbeck-Holloway Center for Entrepreneurial Studies) is the movement's founding text
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Search Fund: Stanford's Signature Entrepreneurial Path

nodes.label: A 2024 GSB study of 681 North American search funds found an aggregate pre-tax return of about 35% a year
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Search Fund: Stanford's Signature Entrepreneurial Path

nodes.label: The MBA Fund — a spring competition where a dozen-odd student startups pitch live to real investors for up to roughly $525K in uncapped SAFEs
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: The venture funds themselves run competitions of their own — SAFEs (often $100K-plus) and sometimes no-strings checks; all the major funds run scout or fellowship programs; watch Blast in the fall
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: Breakthrough — a student-run demo day whose founders have gone on to raise tens of millions
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: Cardinal Ventures — the official student accelerator; non-dilutive builder grants and a Demo Day
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: The BASES $100K Challenge — the campus's decades-old marquee competition (Sam Altman won it in 2005)
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: Venture fellowships — the Sarah Smith GSB Venture Fellowship and Threshold Venture Fellows place you inside a fund for a summer
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: The class angel funds — each MBA class raises its own fund (the "26 Fund," the "27 Fund") on AngelList and backs classmates' startups; the '26 fund deployed roughly $2 million
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: Summer stipends — ESIP (entrepreneurial), SMIF (social-impact), and EcoSIP (climate) will pay you to intern at a startup, nonprofit, or your own project; one application, deadline in late May — the money has run out early before, so apply the moment it opens
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: The impact track: the student-managed GSB Impact Fund recruits new investors each spring
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: The Center for Social Innovation awards graduating fellowships: the Stanford Impact Founder fellowship (recently up to $110K), the Impact Leader prize, and Board Fellows
nodes.source_location: Careers — Getting Funded: Competitions, Grants, and Summer Money

nodes.label: Fall, first year: employer events for MBA1s open in late October (MBA2s' start about a month earlier); consulting and banking front-load here with presentations, coffee chats, and club prep through autumn
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Recruiting Calendar, in Practice

nodes.label: January: the GSB's dedicated on-campus internship interview days for MBA1s — the structured-track crunch, with club guides and CMC mocks for exactly this month
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Recruiting Calendar, in Practice

nodes.label: Spring: tech and most operating roles hire later and role-by-role; startup and VC internships often close in spring — or never formally open at all
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Recruiting Calendar, in Practice

nodes.label: Fall, second year: dedicated full-time interview days in October for MBA2s, alongside return-offer decisions from summer employers
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Recruiting Calendar, in Practice

nodes.label: The honest caveat: a large share of GSB recruiting never touches this published calendar — the school's small-class, network-first, startup-heavy culture means many of the best outcomes are assembled through outreach, not scheduled interviews; treat the calendar as the floor, not the map
nodes.source_location: Careers — The Recruiting Calendar, in Practice

nodes.label: The GSB publishes annual employment reports; the Class of 2025 edition (Clear Admit's summary, Poets&Quants) is a useful calibration
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: Median base salary $185,000 (flat at the school's all-time high; average ~$190,900)
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: About half of Class of 2025 reported signing bonuses, with a median of $30,000
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: Median expected performance bonus of $43,000
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: Technology edged finance for the top industry, 35% vs. 33%, with consulting third — summer internships showed the same AI-driven tech resurgence
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: The timing truth: only ~66% had offers at graduation; within three months it was 90%, with 81% accepted — a June without an offer is a normal chapter of many good stories here, not a verdict
nodes.source_location: Careers — What the Outcomes Data Says

nodes.label: Daily, 11:30–1:15 — Town Square: the whole school idles, eats, and chats in one place; a hundred-plus people gathered casually with nowhere better to be, rarer after graduation than any marquee event
Tuesday — FOAM ("Friends of Arjay Miller"): the recurring happy hour, with drink deals at rotating local bars and several large destination events a year
Wednesday — MBA TALKs: two classmates each tell a ~30-minute story of their life, open to everyone including partners; "go to TALK, even if you're sleepy or on the fence"

Thursday — Beer Pong League (BPL): commissioners run a 10-match regular season plus a playoff bracket in the back area of the Patio — ~25 tables for two hours, then everyone moves inside to the dance floor
"Ten years from now you won't remember anything you learned studying for D&D. But you'll remember this Thursday night." — Helen Cashman
Friday — LPF happy hours and Social Committee parties (usually Fridays; some ticketed for capacity, many free)

Saturday and Sunday are choose-your-own-adventure days: social life is less concentrated on weekends — plenty of people travel or take weekend trips, plenty of others stay back for homework, errands, and recruiting
Daytime, every day: brown-bag lunches and club events with speakers, open to all

FOAM membership math: (1) without a membership you can't attend several big FOAM events that have actual security; (2) the price is the same whenever you buy, so waiting just raises your per-event cost; (3) even non-drinkers find it worth it if attending ~2 major FOAMs a year given venue/food costs; TL;DR: unless impervious to FOMO, do it
nodes.source_location: Social Life — FOAM Membership: Buy or Not?

nodes.label: FOAM stands for "Friends of Arjay Miller" — the beloved dean who ran the GSB from 1969 to 1979, a former president of Ford Motor Company who used to turn up at student spaghetti dinners; admiring students started a drinking club in his honor and the name stuck
nodes.source_location: Social Life — FOAM Membership: Buy or Not?

nodes.label: Confusingly, "Arjay Miller" also names the school's top academic honor (Arjay Miller Scholars, the top ten percent of each graduating class) — same man, two very different distinctions
nodes.source_location: Social Life — FOAM Membership: Buy or Not?

nodes.label: A word on money: headline experiences (Vegas FOAM, the Coachella pilgrimage, far-flung treks) are wonderful and expensive but not mandatory — much of the best of GSB costs little or nothing: talks, dinners, TALK, office hours, a sunrise walk up the Dish, a potluck, a night in someone's backyard; the financial-aid office and Chapter 5's relief valves exist for exactly this
nodes.source_location: Social Life — FOAM Membership: Buy or Not?

nodes.label: Stay at the host hotel or one nearby — booking sites' cheaper options carry hidden resort fees that erase the difference, and logistics get much easier when the party is an elevator ride away
Going hotel-less is a genuinely different weekend: no-hotel is better for the plot, a hotel is better for a somewhat more productive Wednesday — you decide what kind of MBA student you are
Weekend brunch buffets mostly don't run on weekdays — don't build your recovery plan around one

Flights home: the 6 a.m. straight-from-the-party flight and the 2–3 p.m. brunch-first flight both have fans; around 12:30 p.m. threads the needle (checkout at 11, ten minutes to the airport, some sleep first); the worst window is 8–10 a.m. — parties end at 3–4 a.m. and you'll sit in the airport, tired and miserable

Classmates have rented club tables at Omnia for afterparties, taken over a Taco Bell Cantina for a chaotic pregame, and hosted birthday pregames in a Bellagio penthouse — the generosity of the class makes the weekend; budget accordingly and say yes

WAAAM — the cross-school Asian-MBA Vegas weekend, typically the first weekend of spring quarter, draws four-hundred-plus MBAs from Asian business-student associations across the top programs, with headliner DJs in recent years; tickets close about a month out; GSB signups run through ABSA
Executive Challenge — a full-day fall MBA1 event (calendared 7:30 a.m.–7:30 p.m., usually done by ~4:30) with MBA2 coaches and real executives judging; attendance is strictly enforced
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: Shenanigans — an old MBA tradition: sections compete all quarter to perform small, pre-planned, harmless disruptions in class; points are logged in a shared doc and posted to #shenanigans; the winning section gets a prize on par with Executive Challenge's; professors mostly play along
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: Shenanigans examples from the class of '26 tracker: wear a t-shirt with a sectionmate's face on it and sit next to them; pop non-alcoholic champagne in class (bonus for pouring a glass); start the wave in your row; arrive late on rollerblades and blade to your seat
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: GSB Show — the annual student sketch/musical comedy production
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: Comedy Night (the stand-up night) — a real stage for classmates' sets, in the warmest room you'll ever play
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: LOWKeynotes — the TED-style student speaker series: "if those give you a stage, TALK gives you a heart"
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: Window Wars — once a year, first-floor residence students cook food in their dorm rooms and "sell" it out their windows
nodes.source_location: Social Life — Traditions You'll Want Context For

nodes.label: Big Game — Stanford vs. Cal, the Saturday at the start of Thanksgiving break, alternating campuses: "go at least once"
